question: A 9-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician by a concerned parent due to "looking unusually tired and having a noticeable paleness to the skin and lips." The child has a poor appetite but no recent infections or diarrhea. A physical exam shows mild pallor but no other notable findings. Lab tests show: - Hemoglobin: 6.2 g/dL - MCHC: 26% - MCH: 16.0 pg - MCV: 70 fL - Reticulocytes: 0.8% - Platelets: 240,000/mm³ - Leukocyte count: 6,000/mm³ - Neutrophils: 58% - Eosinophils: 2% - Lymphocytes: 31% - Monocytes: 9% Serum Iron: 35 mg/dL TIBC: 460 mg/dL (normal 300-350 mg/dL) Percent saturation of transferrin: 7.6% Total serum bilirubin: 0.8 mg/dL The peripheral blood smear reveals pronounced anisocytosis, microcytosis, hypochromia, and poikilocytosis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Explanation This case demonstrates classic iron deficiency anemia in a 9-month-old infant, characterized by microcytic, hypochromic anemia with low serum iron (35 mg/dL), elevated TIBC (460 mg/dL), and low transferrin saturation (7.6%). This typically occurs during the transition to solid foods when dietary iron intake becomes inadequate. Management should focus on iron supplementation and dietary counseling to ensure adequate iron-rich foods. (Choice A) Megaloblastic anemia Megaloblastic anemia presents with macrocytic anemia (elevated MCV >100 fL) due to B12 or folate deficiency, showing hypersegmented neutrophils and oval macrocytes on peripheral smear. This case shows microcytosis (MCV 70 fL), ruling out megaloblastic anemia. (Choice B) Thalassemia minor Thalassemia minor would typically show a microcytic anemia but with normal or elevated serum iron levels, normal or low TIBC, and often a normal or elevated RBC count with target cells on peripheral smear. The low iron and elevated TIBC make iron deficiency more likely. (Choice C) Anemia of chronic disease Anemia of chronic disease typically presents with low serum iron but also low or normal TIBC (unlike the elevated TIBC seen here), and occurs in patients with underlying inflammatory conditions, infections, or chronic diseases - none of which are present in this healthy infant. (Choice D) Iron deficiency anemia This case demonstrates a microcytic, hypochromic anemia with low serum iron and increased TIBC, characteristic of iron deficiency anemia, commonly due to inadequate dietary iron intake in infants. (Choice E) Lead poisoning anemia Lead poisoning can present with microcytic anemia and may show basophilic stippling on peripheral blood smear. However, this case lacks the characteristic stippling and typically occurs in toddlers with environmental exposure rather than dietary deficiency in infants.

question: A 14-month-old boy is brought to his pediatrician by his parents for irritability and refusal to bear weight on his legs for the past 2 weeks. His parents report he has been exclusively fed a commercial soy-based formula since birth and has never received any vitamin supplements. They avoid giving him fruits or vegetables due to food allergy concerns. On examination, he is afebrile and appears irritable when his legs are handled. There is marked tenderness of the lower extremities, and he refuses to stand. There are no petechiae or purpura noted on the skin, but scattered small hemorrhages are observed around hair follicles on his thighs. Radiographs of the lower extremities show a 'Frankel line' (dense zone of provisional calcification) and a subepiphyseal lucency. Laboratory studies show: hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, MCV 74 fL, platelets 310,000/µL, PT 11.8 sec (INR 0.98), aPTT 28 sec, serum calcium 9.4 mg/dL, phosphorus 4.2 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 185 U/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.label: A
answers.text: Perform arthrocentesis of the knee for presumed septic arthritis (0%)

answers.label: B
answers.text: Order bone marrow biopsy to evaluate for malignancy given bone pain and anemia (0%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Administer fresh frozen plasma for presumed coagulopathy (0%)

answers.label: E
answers.text: Initiate oral calcium and vitamin D supplementation for rickets (0%)

explanation: Explanation Infantile scurvy (Barlow's disease) classically presents with irritability, pseudoparalysis due to subperiosteal hemorrhage, and perifollicular hemorrhages in infants fed unsupplemented diets devoid of vitamin C. Radiographic findings include the Frankel line, Trümmerfeld zone, and the Pelkan spur. Vitamin C supplementation results in rapid and complete resolution of symptoms. (Choice A) Perform arthrocentesis of the knee for presumed septic arthritis Septic arthritis typically presents with fever, erythema, warmth, and a single acutely inflamed joint in the context of an infectious source, rather than bilateral extremity tenderness and pseudoparalysis with the dietary history described here. The absence of fever and the symmetric nature of the findings along with the characteristic radiographic pattern and skin changes make septic arthritis unlikely. Joint aspiration carries procedural risks and would not address the underlying nutritional deficiency. (Choice B) Order bone marrow biopsy to evaluate for malignancy given bone pain and anemia While hematologic malignancy can present with bone pain and anemia in children, the clinical constellation here — perifollicular hemorrhages, pseudoparalysis, Frankel line on radiographs, normal coagulation studies, and a dietary history devoid of vitamin C — points strongly to scurvy. Malignancies typically present with additional findings such as leukocytosis or blasts on peripheral smear, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or significant thrombocytopenia, none of which are described here. Pursuing an invasive diagnostic test before a simple, safe empiric treatment would not be appropriate. (Choice C) Begin oral vitamin C supplementation This infant presents with classic infantile scurvy (Barlow's disease), a diagnosis supported by the exclusive formula feeding without vitamin supplementation, absence of fresh fruits or vegetables, perifollicular hemorrhages, pseudoparalysis from subperiosteal hemorrhage causing extreme limb tenderness, microcytic anemia, and pathognomonic radiographic findings including the Frankel line (sclerotic zone of provisional calcification) and subepiphyseal lucency (Trümmerfeld zone). The normal coagulation studies and platelet count exclude primary bleeding disorders. Commercial infant formulas are typically fortified with vitamin C, but if an unsupplemented formula or alternative diet is used without fresh produce, scurvy can develop by 6–12 months of age. Oral vitamin C supplementation (100–300 mg/day in infants) produces dramatic improvement within days to weeks, with resolution of pain, irritability, and radiographic changes. Dietary counseling to ensure adequate vitamin C intake going forward is also essential. (Choice D) Administer fresh frozen plasma for presumed coagulopathy Fresh frozen plasma is used to correct coagulopathy from clotting factor deficiencies. This patient's PT, aPTT, and platelet count are entirely normal, confirming that the coagulation cascade is intact. The hemorrhagic manifestations of scurvy result from structurally deficient collagen in vessel walls, not from deficient coagulation factors, and FFP would provide no benefit. (Choice E) Initiate oral calcium and vitamin D supplementation for rickets Rickets presents with similar radiographic changes at the growth plate but is caused by vitamin D, calcium, or phosphate deficiency. Classic rickets findings include cupping, fraying, and coarse trabeculation of the metaphyses, along with delayed ossification. This patient's normal serum calcium and phosphorus levels, combined with the specific radiographic pattern of a Frankel line with subepiphyseal lucency, are more consistent with scurvy than rickets. Additionally, the perifollicular hemorrhages are pathognomonic for vitamin C deficiency, not seen in rickets.

question: A 32-year-old woman with a history of severe aplastic anemia undergoes allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation from a matched sibling donor. On day 60 post-transplant, she presents with a diffuse pruritic maculopapular rash starting on her palms and soles and spreading to her trunk, accompanied by severe watery diarrhea (over 2 liters per day) not associated with meals, and mild jaundice with lab values shown below. What is the most likely mechanism underlying her symptoms? Hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL Hematocrit 39% Red Blood Cell Count 4.5×10^6/μL White Blood Cell Count 7600 /mm³ Platelet Count 230000 /mm³ Sodium 139 mmol/L Potassium 4.1 mmol/L Chloride 103 mmol/L Bicarbonate 25 mmol/L Blood Urea Nitrogen 15 mg/dL Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL Glucose 96 mg/dL Calcium 9.1 mg/dL Direct Bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL Alkaline Phosphatase 160 U/L AST 185 U/L ALT 210 U/L Infectious Workup Negative for Clostridium difficile and CMV PCR

answers.label: A
answers.text: Neutrophil-mediated tissue damage secondary to bacterial translocation (5.48%)

answers.label: B
answers.text: Cytokine release from activated B cells (5.48%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Autoantibody-mediated immune complex deposition in target organs (0%)

answers.label: E
answers.text: CD8+ T-lymphocyte mediated cytotoxicity against host epithelial cells (83.56%)

explanation: Explanation The patient's presentation with maculopapular rash, profuse watery diarrhea, and liver involvement within 100 days post-allogeneic HSCT is characteristic of acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). This occurs when donor T cells recognize host antigens as foreign, leading to immune-mediated inflammation. Infections have been excluded, and the timeline does not fit conditioning regimen toxicity or post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder. (Choice A) Neutrophil-mediated tissue damage secondary to bacterial translocation While bacterial translocation can occur in immunocompromised transplant patients and cause GI symptoms, the infectious workup was negative. Additionally, acute GVHD is characterized by T-cell mediated cytotoxicity rather than neutrophilic inflammation, and the classic triad of skin, GI, and liver involvement strongly suggests GVHD. (Choice B) Cytokine release from activated B cells While cytokines do play a role in GVHD pathophysiology, B cells are not the primary cellular mediators. Acute GVHD is predominantly a T-cell mediated process where donor CD8+ T cells directly recognize and attack host epithelial cells, with inflammatory cytokines released primarily by activated T cells and macrophages. (Choice C) Direct toxicity from conditioning chemotherapy Conditioning chemotherapy toxicity typically manifests within the first few weeks post-transplant as mucositis and organ toxicity. The presentation at day 60 with the classic triad of maculopapular rash (especially palms/soles), profuse diarrhea, and hepatitis is characteristic of acute GVHD rather than delayed chemotherapy effects. (Choice D) Autoantibody-mediated immune complex deposition in target organs Autoantibodies are not the primary mechanism in acute GVHD. While autoimmune phenomena can occur post-transplant, acute GVHD is driven by donor T-cell recognition of host antigens, not by host antibody production against self-antigens as seen in conditions like autoimmune hepatitis. (Choice E) CD8+ T-lymphocyte mediated cytotoxicity against host epithelial cells This is the primary mechanism of acute GVHD, where donor-derived CD8+ T cells recognize mismatched host antigens and cause direct tissue damage through cytotoxic pathways.

question: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2, who delivered a healthy infant vaginally 36 hours ago, is brought to the emergency department by her partner after experiencing a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. During her pregnancy, she was diagnosed with preeclampsia and managed with labetalol for blood pressure control. Her last prenatal visit two days before delivery showed blood pressure of 152/98 mm Hg and serum creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL. On arrival, she is postictal, confused, with a persistent severe headache and brisk deep tendon reflexes (3+). Her blood pressure is now 168/102 mm Hg, heart rate 92 bpm, and temperature 37.1°C (98.8°F).Laboratory results are shown below. What is the most appropriate next step in management? White Blood Cell Count 7.9 x10³/µL Neutrophils 60% Lymphocytes 30% Monocytes 6% Eosinophils 3% Basophils 1% Red Blood Cell Count 4.4 x10^6/µL Hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL Hematocrit 39% Platelet Count 260 x10³/µL MPV 9.5 fL Serum Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL Urinalysis - Protein 1+ Urinalysis - WBC 0-2 /HPF Urinalysis - RBC 0-2 /HPF Urinalysis - Nitrite Negative Urinalysis - Leukocyte Esterase Negative Urinalysis - Appearance Clear

answers.label: A
answers.text: Immediate computed tomography of the head (14.29%)

explanation: Explanation This postpartum patient presents with classic signs of eclampsia: generalized tonic-clonic seizure in the setting of preeclampsia with severe features (persistent severe hypertension >160/110 mmHg, elevated creatinine >1.1 mg/dL). The postictal state with severe headache and hyperreflexia (3+) supports this diagnosis. Magnesium sulfate infusion is the first-line treatment for preventing recurrent eclamptic seizures and should be initiated immediately, with concurrent blood pressure management as needed. (Choice A) Immediate computed tomography of the head While head CT may be indicated to rule out intracranial hemorrhage or other CNS pathology, especially if the patient doesn't respond appropriately to treatment, the clinical presentation is classic for postpartum eclampsia. Immediate seizure prophylaxis with magnesium sulfate takes priority over imaging in a hemodynamically stable patient. (Choice B) Intravenous labetalol While labetalol is appropriate for blood pressure control in severe preeclampsia/eclampsia and should be considered as an additional intervention, it does not address the primary concern of seizure prevention and recurrence in this patient who has already had an eclamptic seizure. (Choice C) Phenytoin infusion Phenytoin is a second-line anticonvulsant that may be considered if magnesium sulfate fails or is contraindicated. However, magnesium sulfate remains the first-line treatment for eclamptic seizures due to superior efficacy in preventing recurrent seizures and its additional benefits in preeclampsia management. (Choice D) Lorazepam intravenous bolus Lorazepam is appropriate for acute seizure termination if the patient were actively seizing, but this patient is postictal. For preventing recurrent eclamptic seizures, magnesium sulfate is the standard of care due to its proven efficacy and safety profile in obstetric patients. (Choice E) Magnesium sulfate infusion Magnesium sulfate is the treatment of choice for preventing recurrent seizures in eclampsia, including in the postpartum period.

question: A 68-year-old woman with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is admitted to the intensive care unit for acute respiratory failure due to a severe exacerbation. She is intubated orotracheally to provide mechanical ventilation. Immediately after intubation, the nurse notes that breath sounds are markedly diminished on the left side of the chest, while they are normal on the right. The patient's oxygen saturation drops to 88% despite 100% FiO2, and the right chest appears hyperinflated on percussion. What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?
explanation: Explanation The patient's presentation is consistent with right mainstem bronchus intubation, leading to underventilation of the left lung and overinflation of the right lung. Repositioning the endotracheal tube by withdrawing it slightly will restore bilateral breath sounds and improve oxygenation. (Choice A) Administer nebulized albuterol While albuterol is appropriate for COPD exacerbations, the immediate presentation of asymmetric breath sounds with diminished sounds on the left and hyperinflation on the right immediately post-intubation indicates malpositioned endotracheal tube rather than bronchospasm. Bronchodilators would not correct mechanical ventilation of only one lung. (Choice B) Switch to non-invasive ventilation Switching to non-invasive ventilation would be inappropriate as the patient was intubated for severe respiratory failure and acute decompensation. Additionally, this would not address the underlying problem of malpositioned endotracheal tube, and removing mechanical ventilation support could worsen the patient's respiratory status. (Choice C) Insert a left-sided chest tube While chest tube insertion would be appropriate for pneumothorax (which can cause diminished breath sounds), the clinical picture of hyperinflation on the right side with diminished sounds on the left immediately after intubation is classic for right mainstem bronchus intubation, not pneumothorax. Pneumothorax would typically cause hyperresonance and diminished sounds on the same side. (Choice D) Reposition the endotracheal tube The asymmetric breath sounds and desaturation indicate right mainstem intubation; withdrawing the tube slightly will allow ventilation of both lungs. (Choice E) Perform emergent bronchoscopy Bronchoscopy could evaluate airway issues, but it is not the immediate step for suspected mainstem intubation, which can be corrected by simple repositioning.

question: A 22-year-old college student presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of high fever, dry cough, and increasing shortness of breath. He is tachypneic with a respiratory rate of 36 breaths per minute and appears anxious. Auscultation of the lungs reveals diffuse crackles bilaterally. Laboratory results are shown below. Which of the following best describes this patient's acid-base disorder? White Blood Cell Count (WBC) 7.2×109/L Red Blood Cell Count (RBC) 4.85×1012/L Hemoglobin (Hgb) 14.4 g/dL Hematocrit (Hct) 43.0 % Platelet Count 240×109/L pH (Arterial) 7.49. PaCO2​ (Arterial) 30 mm Hg PaO2​ (Arterial) 65 mm Hg Bicarbonate (HCO3−​) 24 mEq/L

answers.label: B
answers.text: Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic alkalosis (3.03%)

explanation: Explanation This patient's presentation is consistent with acute pneumonia causing hyperventilation, leading to primary respiratory alkalosis. The blood gas values of pH 7.49, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, and HCO3- 24 mEq/L indicate respiratory alkalosis without renal compensation, as the bicarbonate level remains near normal in this acute setting. (Choice A) Respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation This is incorrect. With chronic respiratory alkalosis and renal compensation, HCO3- would be significantly decreased (typically 2-4 mEq/L decrease for every 10 mm Hg decrease in PaCO2). For a PaCO2 of 30 mm Hg (10 mm Hg below normal 40), expected HCO3- would be around 19-22 mEq/L, with pH closer to normal. Here, HCO3- remains at 24 mEq/L and pH is elevated at 7.49, indicating an acute, uncompensated state. (Choice B) Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic alkalosis This is incorrect. Mixed respiratory and metabolic alkalosis would show high pH (>7.45), low PaCO2 (<35 mm Hg), and elevated HCO3- (>26 mEq/L). The normal HCO3- (24 mEq/L) rules out a concurrent metabolic alkalosis component. (Choice C) Respiratory alkalosis without renal compensation This is correct. The high pH and low PaCO2 indicate primary respiratory alkalosis due to hyperventilation from pneumonia. The normal HCO3- shows that renal compensation (HCO3- excretion) has not yet occurred, consistent with an acute process. (Choice D) Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation This is incorrect. Compensated metabolic alkalosis would have high HCO3- (>26 mEq/L) and high PaCO2 (>45 mm Hg), with pH closer to normal (7.40-7.45). The low PaCO2 (30 mm Hg) and normal HCO3- (24 mEq/L) do not fit this pattern. (Choice E) Respiratory acidosis with renal compensation This is incorrect. Compensated respiratory acidosis would have high PaCO2 (>45 mm Hg), elevated HCO3- (>26 mEq/L), and near-normal pH (7.35-7.45). The low PaCO2 (30 mm Hg) and elevated pH (7.49) are inconsistent with any form of respiratory acidosis.

question: A 29-year-old man with a 6-year history of Crohn's disease primarily involving the terminal ileum presents for a follow-up visit. Despite being in clinical remission on adalimumab, he reports chronic fatigue and tingling in his fingertips and toes. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, MCV 104 fL, serum vitamin B12 142 pg/mL (normal 200–900), folate 6.2 ng/mL (normal), albumin 3.4 g/dL, and fecal fat positive. He underwent a 30 cm terminal ileal resection two years ago. He also reports three to five loose stools per day with occasional greasy appearance. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this patient's vitamin B12 deficiency?

answers.label: A
answers.text: Bile acid malabsorption from terminal ileal disease preventing micellar solubilization of vitamin B12 (0%)

answers.label: B
answers.text: Adalimumab-induced suppression of intestinal B12 transport proteins as an adverse effect of biologic therapy (0%)

answers.label: C
answers.text: Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells reducing intrinsic factor production and preventing vitamin B12 binding in the stomach (33.33%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Loss of terminal ileal cubilin receptors from surgical resection and active Crohn's disease eliminating the exclusive absorption site for the vitamin B12-intrinsic factor complex (66.67%)

answers.label: E
answers.text: Proximal jejunal inflammation from Crohn's disease impairing folate absorption and indirectly causing functional B12 deficiency through the methylfolate trap (0%)

explanation: Explanation Vitamin B12 absorption requires binding to intrinsic factor in the stomach and subsequent absorption via specific cubilin receptors exclusively in the terminal ileum. Crohn's disease affecting or surgically resecting the terminal ileum eliminates this absorption site, causing B12 deficiency regardless of dietary intake. Parenteral or high-dose oral B12 supplementation is required. (Choice A) Bile acid malabsorption from terminal ileal disease preventing micellar solubilization of vitamin B12 Bile acid malabsorption from terminal ileal disease does occur in this patient (evidenced by steatorrhea) and impairs fat-soluble vitamin absorption (A, D, E, K) by preventing micelle formation. However, vitamin B12 is water-soluble and does not require bile acid micellar solubilization for absorption. B12 absorption depends specifically on binding to cubilin receptors in the terminal ileum after complexing with intrinsic factor. The patient's B12 deficiency results from loss of these specialized receptors, not from bile acid malabsorption. (Choice B) Adalimumab-induced suppression of intestinal B12 transport proteins as an adverse effect of biologic therapy Adalimumab, a TNF-alpha inhibitor, does not impair vitamin B12 absorption and has no known direct effect on intestinal B12 transport. The B12 deficiency in this patient is clearly attributable to terminal ileal Crohn's disease and surgical resection eliminating cubilin receptor-mediated B12 absorption, not to biologic therapy. (Choice C) Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells reducing intrinsic factor production and preventing vitamin B12 binding in the stomach This mechanism describes pernicious anemia, an autoimmune condition where antibodies destroy gastric parietal cells, leading to intrinsic factor deficiency. While pernicious anemia causes identical B12 deficiency symptoms, this patient's deficiency results from terminal ileal Crohn's disease and surgical resection that eliminated the absorption site for the IF-B12 complex. The patient likely has normal intrinsic factor production. Pernicious anemia would be diagnosed by elevated methylmalonic acid, low or absent intrinsic factor levels, and positive anti-intrinsic factor or anti-parietal cell antibodies. (Choice D) Loss of terminal ileal cubilin receptors from surgical resection and active Crohn's disease eliminating the exclusive absorption site for the vitamin B12-intrinsic factor complex Vitamin B12 absorption is a highly site-specific process. After ingestion, B12 is released from food proteins by gastric acid and pepsin, then bound by intrinsic factor (IF) secreted by gastric parietal cells. The IF-B12 complex travels to the terminal ileum, where it binds to specific cubilin receptors for endocytosis and absorption. The terminal ileum is the only site in the gastrointestinal tract capable of absorbing the IF-B12 complex. This patient's Crohn's disease affecting the terminal ileum combined with a 30 cm resection has destroyed and eliminated this exclusive absorption site. Even with adequate dietary B12 intake and normal intrinsic factor production, B12 cannot be absorbed without functional terminal ileal mucosa. The result is B12 deficiency causing macrocytic anemia (MCV 104 fL) and peripheral neuropathy (tingling in the extremities reflecting subacute combined degeneration). Treatment requires lifelong parenteral B12 supplementation or high-dose oral B12 (1000 mcg daily) relying on passive diffusion. (Choice E) Proximal jejunal inflammation from Crohn's disease impairing folate absorption and indirectly causing functional B12 deficiency through the methylfolate trap The methylfolate trap occurs when B12 deficiency prevents conversion of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, causing functional folate deficiency despite adequate folate intake. However, this patient has normal serum folate levels, indicating the methylfolate trap is not occurring. Additionally, the proximal jejunum is the primary site of folate absorption, not B12 absorption, which occurs exclusively in the terminal ileum. The patient's B12 deficiency is primary (due to terminal ileal disease), not secondary to folate metabolism dysfunction.

question: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents after they observed bright red blood mixed with her stool during a routine diaper change. The episode occurred without any preceding abdominal pain, vomiting, or changes in bowel habits. The child appears well-nourished, active, and in no distress. Physical examination reveals normal vital signs, a soft and nontender abdomen, and no signs of dehydration. Laboratory tests are shown below. What is the most appropriate diagnostic test to confirm the suspected underlying condition? White blood cells 7800 /mm3 Neutrophils 60 % Lymphocytes 30 % Monocytes 6 % Eosinophils 3 % Basophils 1 % Hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL Hematocrit 32 % Mean corpuscular volume 88 fL Platelets 250000 /μL Prothrombin time 12 sec INR 1.0 Activated partial thromboplastin time 32 sec
explanation: Explanation This toddler presents with painless rectal bleeding suggestive of Meckel diverticulum, a congenital remnant of the vitelline duct that may contain ectopic gastric mucosa leading to ulceration and hemorrhage. The technetium-99m pertechnetate scan is the preferred diagnostic modality as it specifically identifies ectopic gastric tissue. Other options like CT scan, ultrasound, stool culture, upper endoscopy, air contrast enema, and colonoscopy are less specific or inappropriate for initial diagnosis of Meckel diverticulum in this context. (Choice A) Technetium-99m pertechnetate scan This is the correct diagnostic test as it detects ectopic gastric mucosa in Meckel diverticulum with high sensitivity and specificity, confirming the cause of painless bleeding. (Choice B) Colonoscopy Colonoscopy can evaluate the colon for polyps or inflammation but is invasive and unlikely to visualize a Meckel diverticulum located in the ileum. (Choice C) Air contrast enema Air contrast enema is used for diagnosing and reducing intussusception, which typically presents with intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, and currant jelly stools - features absent in this painless presentation. (Choice D) Bacterial stool culture Stool culture is indicated for infectious diarrhea, but this patient has no diarrhea, fever, or signs of infection. (Choice E) Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy Upper endoscopy evaluates the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum but cannot reach a Meckel diverticulum located in the distal small bowel (ileum).

question: A 62-year-old man with recently diagnosed non-small cell lung cancer presents for follow-up after starting chemotherapy. He reports profound fatigue, a 12-pound unintentional weight loss over the past month, difficulty sleeping, and poor concentration. He also states that he has lost interest in spending time with his grandchildren, which he previously enjoyed immensely, and feels persistently sad and worthless. These symptoms have persisted for 4 weeks despite stable imaging showing no disease progression. His medications include only chemotherapy agents and supportive care drugs. What is the most likely diagnosis contributing to this patient's symptoms?
explanation: Explanation This patient's symptoms of persistent fatigue, weight loss, insomnia, impaired concentration, anhedonia, and depressed mood lasting >2 weeks are suggestive of major depressive disorder (MDD) rather than solely cancer-related effects or treatment side effects. The presence of core depressive features like loss of interest and depressed mood in conjunction with somatic symptoms supports considering MDD, which can coexist with cancer and requires targeted management to improve quality of life and adherence. (Choice A) Adjustment disorder with depressed mood Adjustment disorder with depressed mood occurs within 6 months of a stressor and involves emotional symptoms, but this patient meets criteria for major depressive disorder due to the presence of core symptoms (depressed mood, anhedonia) plus additional criteria (sleep, concentration, weight loss, worthlessness) persisting >2 weeks with significant functional impairment. (Choice B) Generalized anxiety disorder Although generalized anxiety disorder can present with sleep disturbances and concentration difficulties, this patient's predominant symptoms are depressive (anhedonia, persistent sadness, worthlessness) rather than anxiety-related (excessive worry, restlessness, muscle tension). (Choice C) Major depressive disorder The patient's symptoms meet criteria for major depressive disorder, including depressed mood, anhedonia, and somatic symptoms lasting >2 weeks, which are not fully explained by cancer or treatment alone. (Choice D) Chemotherapy-induced neurotoxicity Chemotherapy can cause fatigue and cognitive issues, but it does not typically produce core depressive symptoms like anhedonia and feelings of worthlessness. (Choice E) Cancer-related fatigue While cancer-related fatigue is common and this patient does have fatigue, the constellation of symptoms including anhedonia (loss of interest in grandchildren), persistent sadness, feelings of worthlessness, and duration >2 weeks indicates a mood disorder rather than isolated fatigue syndrome.

question: A 3-day-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician for evaluation of lethargy and difficulty feeding since birth. She was born at 39 weeks' gestation to a 42-year-old mother via spontaneous vaginal delivery. Pregnancy was uncomplicated, but prenatal screening was declined. On examination, the infant weighs 2.6 kg (5th percentile), has a flat occiput, epicanthal folds, a protruding tongue, and loose skin at the nape of the neck. She exhibits generalized hypotonia, a weak cry, and a single transverse crease on each palm. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Explanation This neonate presents with characteristic features of Down syndrome, including hypotonia, poor feeding, macroglossia, epicanthal folds, flat occiput, nuchal skin redundancy, single palmar creases, and a heart murmur suggestive of a congenital defect. The condition is caused by trisomy 21, confirmed by karyotype analysis. (Choice A) Prader-Willi syndrome This is incorrect. Prader-Willi syndrome presents with neonatal hypotonia and feeding difficulties, but the characteristic facial features include almond-shaped eyes, narrow bifrontal diameter, and down-turned mouth. It lacks the epicanthal folds, protruding tongue, and single palmar creases seen in this case. It is due to deletion or imprinting defects on chromosome 15q11-q13. (Choice B) Noonan syndrome This is incorrect. Noonan syndrome may include congenital heart defects, short stature, and webbed neck, but the characteristic facial features include prominent forehead, hypertelorism, ptosis, and low-set posteriorly rotated ears. The profound neonatal hypotonia, epicanthal folds, protruding tongue, and single palmar creases are not typical of Noonan syndrome. It is caused by mutations affecting the RAS-MAPK pathway. (Choice C) Trisomy 18 This is incorrect. Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) features severe intrauterine growth restriction, characteristic clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, and severe congenital heart defects. While growth restriction is present in this case, the specific dysmorphic features (epicanthal folds, protruding tongue, single palmar creases) are not characteristic of Edwards syndrome. (Choice D) Down syndrome This is the correct diagnosis. The infant's features, including hypotonia, dysmorphic facial characteristics, single palmar creases, and heart murmur, are classic for Down syndrome, which is caused by trisomy 21 in most cases. (Choice E) Congenital hypothyroidism This is incorrect. Congenital hypothyroidism can cause hypotonia, poor feeding, and macroglossia, but typically presents with prolonged physiologic jaundice, large posterior fontanelle, and coarse facial features. It does not cause the specific dysmorphic features seen here (epicanthal folds, flat occiput, single palmar creases) which are pathognomonic for a chromosomal disorder.

question: A 70-year-old woman presents with a persistent, non-healing sore on her left cheek that has been increasing in size over the last eight months. Upon examination, the lesion is a firm, roughened plaque with central ulceration, measuring about 2 cm in diameter. Histological analysis reveals disorganized keratinocytes with atypical nuclei throughout the epidermis, alongside areas of keratin pearl formation. What is the primary environmental factor contributing to this condition?
explanation: Explanation This case exemplifies squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) on a chronically sun-exposed area. UV radiation is widely recognized as the foremost environmental contributor to skin cancers due to its DNA-damaging effects. Prevention includes sun protection and regular dermatological evaluations. (Choice A) Occupational chemical exposure While certain occupational chemical exposures (such as arsenic, coal tar, and petroleum products) can increase SCC risk, these exposures are less common and not the primary environmental risk factor compared to ubiquitous UV radiation exposure. (Choice B) Human papillomavirus infection While HPV infection is associated with some SCCs, particularly in mucosal and anogenital sites, it is not the primary environmental risk factor for cutaneous SCCs on sun-exposed areas like the face. UV radiation remains the dominant risk factor for facial skin cancers. (Choice C) Chronic wound presence Tobacco use is a significant risk factor for mucosal SCCs, particularly in the oral cavity, oropharynx, and respiratory tract, but is not the primary environmental risk factor for cutaneous SCCs on sun-exposed skin surfaces. (Choice D) Tobacco use Tobacco use is a significant risk factor for mucosal SCCs, particularly in the oral cavity and lungs, but not as strongly linked to skin carcinomas. (Choice E) Ultraviolet radiation from sun exposure Prolonged sun exposure is the primary environmental risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). The UV light causes DNA damage, inducing mutations that can lead to malignancy.

question: A 44-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a BMI of 33 kg/m² presents for a routine follow-up. His LDL is 146 mg/dL, blood pressure is 144/88 mmHg, and fasting glucose is 104 mg/dL. He reports eating red meat five to six times per week, processed deli meats daily, and minimal fruits or vegetables. He recently read about climate change and asks his physician whether his diet has any environmental impact. He is motivated to make changes but asks whether dietary modifications that help the environment would also benefit his health. Which of the following best describes the relationship between reduced red and processed meat consumption and both personal health and environmental outcomes?

answers.label: A
answers.text: The patient should adopt a fully vegan diet immediately to achieve maximum environmental and health benefits, as partial reductions in animal product consumption have negligible impact (0%)

answers.label: B
answers.text: Individual dietary choices have minimal environmental impact compared to industrial sources, and environmental counseling is not within the physician's scope of practice (0%)

answers.label: C
answers.text: Reducing red and processed meat consumption lowers LDL cholesterol, blood pressure, and colorectal cancer risk while simultaneously reducing greenhouse gas emissions, land use, and water consumption — representing a convergent benefit for both personal and planetary health (100%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Plant-based meat alternatives provide identical health and environmental benefits to whole plant foods when replacing red meat (0%)

answers.label: E
answers.text: Grass-fed organic beef is nutritionally and environmentally equivalent to plant-based proteins and can be freely recommended as a sustainable heart-healthy protein source (0%)

explanation: Explanation Reducing red and processed meat consumption simultaneously addresses cardiovascular risk factors and environmental sustainability. Beef production generates approximately 20 times more greenhouse gas emissions per gram of protein than plant-based proteins and requires substantially more land and water. Processed meat is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the IARC. Replacing red and processed meat with plant-based proteins reduces LDL, blood pressure, and colorectal cancer risk while dramatically reducing dietary carbon footprint. (Choice A) The patient should adopt a fully vegan diet immediately to achieve maximum environmental and health benefits, as partial reductions in animal product consumption have negligible impact While fully plant-based diets do maximize environmental sustainability benefits, even partial reductions in red and processed meat consumption produce meaningful and proportional health and environmental benefits. Evidence from the Nurses' Health Study and Health Professionals Follow-up Study demonstrates dose-response relationships between red meat reduction and cardiovascular risk. Similarly, environmental analyses show that replacing beef with chicken, fish, or plant proteins at even a few meals per week produces meaningful reductions in dietary carbon footprint. Prescribing complete veganism as the only acceptable dietary goal is impractical for most patients and may produce all-or-nothing thinking leading to complete disengagement. Practical, achievable partial reductions are more effective counseling targets. (Choice B) Individual dietary choices have minimal environmental impact compared to industrial sources, and environmental counseling is not within the physician's scope of practice This choice incorrectly dismisses both the environmental impact of individual dietary choices and the role of physicians in sustainability counseling. Individual food choices, when aggregated, represent one of the largest modifiable drivers of greenhouse gas emissions from the food system, which accounts for 21-37% of global emissions. Animal agriculture, particularly beef production, contributes disproportionately to these emissions. Medical organizations including the American College of Physicians and World Medical Association now recognize environmental sustainability as interconnected with health outcomes and support incorporating these dimensions into patient care. This represents an evolution in medical practice recognizing planetary health as a determinant of human health. (Choice C) Reducing red and processed meat consumption lowers LDL cholesterol, blood pressure, and colorectal cancer risk while simultaneously reducing greenhouse gas emissions, land use, and water consumption — representing a convergent benefit for both personal and planetary health This patient presents an opportunity to counsel on the co-benefits of dietary change for personal and environmental health — a growing area of clinical relevance as patients increasingly ask about the intersection of dietary choices and sustainability. Personal health benefits of reducing red and processed meat: (1) Cardiovascular risk reduction: red meat is high in saturated fat (primarily palmitic and stearic acid) that downregulates hepatic LDL receptor expression, raising this patient's already elevated LDL. Processed meats including deli meats contain high sodium (contributing to his uncontrolled hypertension), saturated fat, and nitrate preservatives associated with endothelial dysfunction. Replacing red meat with plant-based proteins reduces LDL by 5–10% and blood pressure through sodium reduction. (2) Cancer risk: the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies processed meat as a Group 1 carcinogen (sufficient evidence of carcinogenicity in humans) and red meat as a Group 2A probable carcinogen, with strongest evidence for colorectal cancer risk. Each 50g daily increment of processed meat increases colorectal cancer risk by approximately 18%. (3) Metabolic benefits: plant-based protein replacements from legumes, nuts, and whole grains improve insulin sensitivity and reduce fasting glucose — relevant to this patient's prediabetes (glucose 104). Environmental benefits of reducing red and processed meat: Beef production is among the most environmentally intensive food sources globally — generating approximately 20 times more greenhouse gas emissions per gram of protein than legumes, requiring 20 times more land, and consuming vastly more water. Cattle are responsible for approximately 14.5% of global anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions through methane production (enteric fermentation), nitrous oxide from manure, and carbon dioxide from land use change including deforestation. Processed meat manufacturing adds additional energy and resource costs. Shifting even partially toward plant-based proteins represents one of the highest-impact individual dietary changes for environmental sustainability. The EAT-Lancet Commission's Planetary Health Diet recommends a dramatic reduction in red meat consumption globally to simultaneously address non-communicable disease burden and environmental sustainability targets. (Choice D) Plant-based meat alternatives provide identical health and environmental benefits to whole plant foods when replacing red meat Ultraprocessed plant-based meat alternatives — while generally lower in greenhouse gas emissions than beef — are not equivalent to whole food plant-based substitution in health outcomes. Many commercial plant-based burgers and processed meat alternatives contain high sodium (400–600 mg per serving), saturated fat from coconut oil, and numerous food additives associated with adverse health outcomes in epidemiological studies. The health benefits of reducing red meat are maximized by replacing it with whole plant foods including legumes, nuts, seeds, and whole grains — not by substituting one ultraprocessed product for another. Environmental benefits are better achieved with whole plant foods than ultraprocessed alternatives, which carry significant manufacturing energy costs. (Choice E) Grass-fed organic beef is nutritionally and environmentally equivalent to plant-based proteins and can be freely recommended as a sustainable heart-healthy protein source This choice incorrectly equates grass-fed beef with plant-based proteins for both health and environmental outcomes. While grass-fed beef has marginally higher omega-3 fatty acids compared to grain-fed beef, it still contains significant saturated fat that contributes to this patient's elevated LDL cholesterol. Environmentally, grass-fed beef actually requires more land and time to produce than grain-fed beef, and still generates 15-20 times more greenhouse gas emissions per gram of protein than legumes. The slight nutritional differences do not offset the substantial cardiovascular risk from saturated fat intake or the environmental impact compared to plant-based alternatives.

question: A 38-year-old Caucasian woman presents to the emergency department with a sudden severe headache, nausea, vomiting, and blurred vision. She denies any history of trauma, migraines, or recent infections. She is not taking oral contraceptives and has no history of malignancy or autoimmune diseases. Her family history includes a brother who experienced an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis at age 35. Neurological examination reveals papilledema, and CT venography confirms thrombosis in the superior sagittal sinus. Laboratory tests are shown below. Which of the following is the most likely underlying abnormality contributing to her condition? Hemoglobin 14 g/dL Hematocrit 42 % WBC 7.0x10^3/µL Platelets 250x10^3/µL MCV 90 fL MCH 30 pg MCHC 33 g/dL RDW 12 % PT 12 seconds (range: 11-13.5 seconds) INR 1.0 (range:0.8-1.2 ) aPTT 32 seconds (range:25-35 seconds) D-dimer 0.2 mg/L (normal< 0.5 mg/L) Anticardiolipin antibodies Negative Beta-2 glycoprotein antibodies Negative Lupus anticoagulant Negative
explanation: Explanation This patient presents with cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, an unusual site for thrombosis, in a young Caucasian individual without provoking factors and a positive family history of unprovoked venous thrombosis. The most common hereditary thrombophilia in Caucasians is factor V Leiden mutation (affecting 3-8% of the population), which causes resistance to activated protein C and significantly increases the risk of venous thromboembolism, particularly at unusual sites. (Choice A) Hyperhomocysteinemia Hyperhomocysteinemia can be inherited (MTHFR mutations, cystathionine β-synthase deficiency) or acquired (B12/folate deficiency) and does increase thrombosis risk. However, inherited forms are less common than factor V Leiden, and acquired forms would likely present with additional findings like megaloblastic anemia or neurological symptoms. (Choice B) Activated protein C resistance Factor V Leiden mutation leads to activated protein C resistance, which is the most common inherited thrombophilia in Caucasians and predisposes to venous thrombosis, especially in unusual sites like cerebral veins in young patients without other risk factors. (Choice C) Prothrombin G20210A mutation Prothrombin G20210A mutation is indeed the second most common inherited thrombophilia in Caucasians (2-3% prevalence) and increases prothrombin levels, leading to hypercoagulability. While this could cause cerebral venous thrombosis, factor V Leiden remains more prevalent (3-8%) and is the most likely cause in this clinical scenario. (Choice D) Protein S deficiency Protein S deficiency is an inherited thrombophilia that increases venous thrombosis risk, including unusual sites like cerebral veins. However, it affects only 0.03-0.13% of the population, making it much less likely than factor V Leiden (3-8% prevalence) in a Caucasian patient with unprovoked thrombosis. (Choice E) Antithrombin III deficiency Antithrombin III deficiency is a less common inherited thrombophilia that causes severe thrombotic risk and typically presents with recurrent thromboses from a young age. While it can cause cerebral venous thrombosis, it affects only 0.02-0.2% of the population compared to factor V Leiden's 3-8% prevalence in Caucasians.

question: A 55-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presents to the clinic for routine follow-up. He has been increasingly fatigued and mentions concerns about his long-term prognosis. During the visit, he expresses worry that decisions about emergency interventions might lead to reduced attention from his care team. The physician wants to discuss his code status as part of a broader goals-of-care conversation. Which of the following is the most appropriate way for the physician to initiate this discussion?

answers.label: A
answers.text: If your heart stops, we could focus on comfort measures rather than attempting resuscitation; would this be acceptable? (0.87%)

answers.label: B
answers.text: Have you considered whether you'd want us to try restarting your heart if it stops? It won't change how we manage your dialysis. (70.43%)

answers.label: C
answers.text: Most patients with advanced kidney disease choose to focus on comfort rather than aggressive resuscitation; would you prefer this approach? (0.87%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Would you like us to attempt all resuscitative measures if your heart stops? We can adjust your other care based on your preferences. (27.83%)

explanation: Explanation Patients often fear that a do-not-resuscitate order may relegate them to a lower priority for the care team or otherwise compromise their care. To best understand the patients' wishes, code status should be addressed in a broader discussion regarding goals of care, using nonleading questions, avoiding euphemisms, and providing reassurance that their decisions will not otherwise alter their treatment or overall quality of care. (Choice A) If your heart stops, we could focus on comfort measures rather than attempting resuscitation; would this be acceptable? This employs a euphemism ('let nature take its course') and does not provide reassurance about maintaining other aspects of care, potentially reinforcing fears of neglect. (Choice B) Have you considered whether you'd want us to try restarting your heart if it stops? It won't change how we manage your dialysis. This is the most appropriate response as it uses clear, non-euphemistic language, poses a nonleading question, and reassures the patient that his decision won't affect other aspects of his care. (Choice C) Most patients with advanced kidney disease choose to focus on comfort rather than aggressive resuscitation; would you prefer this approach? This presents a leading question that suggests what 'most patients' choose, which may pressure the patient toward a particular decision rather than allowing him to express his authentic preferences. Effective code status discussions should be patient-centered, not influenced by population statistics. (Choice D) Would you like us to attempt all resuscitative measures if your heart stops? We can adjust your other care based on your preferences. This uses vague euphemisms like 'everything possible' and 'things get really bad' that fail to clearly communicate what interventions are being discussed. Additionally, the phrase 'adjust your care accordingly' could reinforce the patient's fear that choosing DNR might compromise his overall medical care.

question: A 52-year-old retail store manager presents with a 4-month history of left heel pain that is most severe in the morning upon first stepping out of bed and worsens after prolonged standing during work shifts. She denies any recent trauma or changes in footwear. Physical examination reveals point tenderness at the anteromedial calcaneus, with no swelling or erythema. A lateral foot radiograph demonstrates a small calcaneal spur. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this patient's condition?

answers.label: C
answers.text: Surgical excision of the calcaneal spur (0%)

explanation: Explanation This patient most likely has plantar fasciitis, a degenerative condition of the plantar aponeurosis caused by repetitive microtrauma and overuse. Initial management includes activity modification, stretching exercises for the plantar fascia and Achilles tendon, and padded heel inserts to reduce strain on the plantar fascia. Calcaneal spurs are incidental radiographic findings that do not cause pain and do not require surgical removal. (Choice A) Corticosteroid injection into the heel Corticosteroid injections are reserved for refractory cases that fail to respond to 6-8 weeks of conservative treatment. First-line risks include plantar fascia rupture, fat pad atrophy, and temporary pain flare, making conservative measures preferable initially. (Choice B) Immediate referral for custom orthotics Custom orthotics may be beneficial but are typically reserved for cases that don't respond to over-the-counter heel inserts and conservative measures after 6-8 weeks. Initial management should start with less expensive, readily available options. (Choice C) Surgical excision of the calcaneal spur Surgical removal is not indicated as first-line treatment. Calcaneal spurs are incidental findings in plantar fasciitis and do not cause the pain - the pain originates from inflammation/degeneration of the plantar fascia itself, not the spur. (Choice D) Prescription nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs While NSAIDs can provide symptomatic pain relief, they do not address the underlying mechanical dysfunction causing plantar fasciitis. The mainstay of treatment focuses on biomechanical correction through heel inserts, stretching, and activity modification. (Choice E) Over-the-counter heel inserts Padded heel inserts are a first-line treatment to reduce strain on the plantar fascia and alleviate pain.

question: A 28-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 6-month history of elevated blood pressure readings, averaging 150/95 mm Hg, despite lifestyle modifications. He reports occasional flank discomfort but no hematuria or urinary symptoms. His medical history is unremarkable, but his mother was diagnosed with chronic kidney disease in her 40s and required dialysis by age 50. Physical examination reveals mild bilateral flank tenderness. Laboratory evaluation shows a serum creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL and normal electrolytes. Renal ultrasound demonstrates enlarged kidneys with numerous bilateral cysts. What is the most likely pathophysiological mechanism underlying this patient's hypertension?

answers.label: C
answers.text: Endothelial dysfunction secondary to uremic toxins (3.77%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Primary aldosterone excess from adrenal adenoma (0%)

explanation: Explanation The patient likely has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Hypertension arises from cyst expansion causing localized renal ischemia, which stimulates increased renin production and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). This mechanism explains the early onset of hypertension in ADPKD, and ACE inhibitors are recommended as first-line therapy. The family history supports the genetic nature of the condition. (Choice A) Increased renin activity Cyst expansion in ADPKD leads to localized renal ischemia, stimulating juxtaglomerular cells to release renin, which activates the RAAS and causes hypertension. (Choice B) Direct vascular compression by cysts While cysts can compress intrarenal blood vessels and nephrons, the predominant mechanism of hypertension in ADPKD is ischemia-induced renin release from the juxtaglomerular apparatus, rather than direct mechanical compression of major renal vessels. (Choice C) Endothelial dysfunction secondary to uremic toxins Uremia occurs in advanced stages of kidney disease, but this patient's creatinine is only mildly elevated, and hypertension in ADPKD precedes significant renal failure. (Choice D) Primary aldosterone excess from adrenal adenoma Primary hyperaldosteronism involves autonomous aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex (usually adenoma or hyperplasia), causing volume expansion and hypertension through mineralocorticoid excess, not the renin-mediated mechanism seen in ADPKD. (Choice E) Increased erythropoietin production Erythropoietin production may be altered in CKD, but elevated EPO does not directly cause hypertension. The hypertension in ADPKD is primarily mediated through RAAS activation from localized renal ischemia.

question: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman presents to the gynecology clinic with a 4-month history of intermittent vaginal spotting, foul-smelling discharge, and mild pelvic discomfort. She reports no recent sexual activity and has not had a Pap smear in over 10 years. Her medical history includes hypertension and a 40-pack-year smoking history. On pelvic examination, a 4-cm exophytic, friable mass is noted on the anterior cervix, with contact bleeding. Biopsy reveals invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Which of the following is the most significant modifiable risk factor associated with this patient's diagnosis?
explanation: Explanation This patient presents with postmenopausal vaginal bleeding, foul discharge, and a friable cervical mass consistent with advanced cervical squamous cell carcinoma. Among the risk factors listed, tobacco use is the most significant modifiable risk factor for cervical cancer, as it impairs immune clearance of HPV infection and directly promotes carcinogenesis through DNA damage and chronic inflammation. (Choice A) Long-term oral contraceptive use Long-term oral contraceptive use (>5 years) is associated with a modest increase in cervical cancer risk, but this patient's history does not mention OCP use. Additionally, tobacco use has a much stronger association with cervical squamous cell carcinoma than OCP use. (Choice B) Tobacco use Tobacco use is a well-established modifiable risk factor for squamous cell cervical carcinoma, as it impairs immune clearance of HPV and promotes carcinogenesis. (Choice C) Hypertension Hypertension is not associated with cervical cancer risk. While hypertension is a cardiovascular risk factor, it does not contribute to HPV-related cervical carcinogenesis or squamous cell transformation. (Choice D) Alcohol consumption Excessive alcohol consumption is linked to liver and other cancers but is not a major risk factor for cervical cancer. (Choice E) Nulliparity Nulliparity (never having given birth) is not mentioned in this patient's history and is not a significant risk factor for cervical squamous cell carcinoma. High parity (multiple pregnancies) is actually associated with increased cervical cancer risk, likely due to hormonal and immunologic changes during pregnancy.

question: A 54-year-old woman presents to the clinic with increasingly impaired gait and persistent pain in her left ankle, which has been a concern over the past two months. Her medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, longstanding hypertension, and dyslipidemia. On examination, there is significant deformity observed in both her ankles, but more pronounced in the left. An X-ray of her left foot reveals joint effusion and large osteophytes with displaced bone fragments around the tibiotalar joint. What is the most likely underlying cause of this woman's symptoms?
explanation: Explanation The patient's symptoms and X-ray findings are indicative of Charcot's joint. Diabetes-induced peripheral neuropathy results in loss of sensation, preventing pain detection, and results in repetitive joint injury and subsequent deformation. Radiographic findings typically include joint effusions, osteophytes, and joint fragmentation. Management involves offloading the affected limb and optimizing glucose control. (Choice A) Vascular insufficiency Vascular insufficiency from peripheral artery disease can cause tissue ischemia and ulcerations in diabetic patients, but it does not directly cause the joint destruction, osteophyte formation, and bone fragmentation seen on this patient's X-ray. (Choice B) Primary osteoarthritis Primary osteoarthritis typically affects weight-bearing joints with gradual joint space narrowing and osteophyte formation, but the acute presentation with extensive joint destruction and bone fragmentation in a diabetic patient is more consistent with neuropathic arthropathy than degenerative joint disease. (Choice C) Bone mineral density loss Osteoporosis causes decreased bone mineral density and predisposes to fractures, but it does not cause the active joint destruction, osteophyte formation, and bone fragmentation seen in this case without associated trauma or underlying joint disease. (Choice D) Rheumatoid arthritis Rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory arthritides typically cause symmetric polyarticular involvement with joint space narrowing, erosions, and soft tissue swelling. The unilateral presentation with extensive osteophyte formation and bone fragmentation is not characteristic of inflammatory joint disease. (Choice E) Peripheral neuropathy In individuals with long-standing diabetes, peripheral neuropathy causes damage to sensory nerves, leading to Charcot's joint or neurogenic arthropathy. Without sensation, continuous trauma to weight-bearing joints goes unnoticed, resulting in deformity and joint destruction.

question: A 35-year-old man with a history of mild hemophilia A presents to the emergency department with severe back pain and hematuria following a minor fall while playing sports. He has been receiving prophylactic factor VIII infusions for the past 5 years due to recurrent joint bleeds. Despite administering his usual dose of factor VIII concentrate immediately after the injury, his symptoms have worsened over the next 24 hours, with increasing pain and visible blood in the urine. Laboratory evaluation is shown below. His hemoglobin level is decreased from his baseline. What is the most likely explanation for his refractory bleeding? Hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL Hematocrit 41 % Red Blood Cell Count 4.8×10^6/μL Mean Corpuscular Volume 86 fL Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin 29 pg Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration 33 g/dL Red Cell Distribution Width 13 % White Blood Cell Count 7200 /μL Neutrophils 58 % Lymphocytes 32 % Monocytes 6 % Eosinophils 3 % Basophils 1 % Platelet Count 250000 /μL Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT) 65 seconds (range: 25–35 seconds) Prothrombin Time (PT) 12 seconds (range: 11–13.5 seconds)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Development of inhibitors against factor VIII (99.08%)

answers.label: E
answers.text: Allergic reaction to factor VIII concentrate (0%)

explanation: Explanation This patient with hemophilia A on factor VIII replacement therapy presents with back pain and hematuria after trauma, with persistent bleeding despite infusions. Labs show prolonged aPTT and normal PT, consistent with inhibitor development against factor VIII, leading to treatment resistance. (Choice A) Progression to acquired hemophilia Acquired hemophilia typically occurs in older adults without prior bleeding history and is caused by spontaneous development of factor VIII inhibitors. This patient has congenital hemophilia A and is developing inhibitors as a complication of treatment, not progressing to a different condition. (Choice B) Vitamin K deficiency Vitamin K deficiency affects PT more than aPTT and would not explain isolated prolonged aPTT or resistance to factor VIII therapy in hemophilia A. (Choice C) Underlying renal cell carcinoma While hematuria after trauma could suggest malignancy, the key clinical clues - known hemophilia A, refractory bleeding despite factor VIII treatment, and isolated prolonged aPTT with normal PT - strongly point to a coagulopathy complication rather than underlying malignancy. (Choice D) Development of inhibitors against factor VIII Inhibitor development is a known complication in hemophilia A patients on replacement therapy, leading to neutralizing antibodies that render factor VIII ineffective, causing refractory bleeding and prolonged aPTT. (Choice E) Allergic reaction to factor VIII concentrate Allergic reactions to factor VIII can occur but typically present with symptoms like rash, urticaria, bronchospasm, or anaphylaxis rather than isolated refractory bleeding with prolonged aPTT. The clinical picture and laboratory findings are inconsistent with an allergic reaction.

question: A 52-year-old construction worker comes to the emergency department experiencing significant pain and warmth in his right foot. He explains that three weeks ago he accidentally stepped on a sharp metal object while working. Despite keeping the wound clean with over-the-counter antiseptics and pain relief using ibuprofen, he notices increasing discomfort and difficulty walking. He is generally healthy, with no chronic conditions and no known allergies. He smokes daily and occasionally consumes alcohol. His temperature registers at 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), with a blood pressure of 130/85 mm Hg, a pulse of 90/min, and respirations of 16/min. Upon examination, the right foot shows pronounced redness, swelling, and tenderness, especially around a minor puncture site. Laboratory tests reveal elevated white blood cell counts. MRI of the foot indicates changes aligned with osteomyelitis. What is the most probable organism responsible for his symptoms?
explanation: Explanation This case illustrates puncture wound osteomyelitis, a specific subset of bone infections. Pseudomonas aeruginosa has a particular predilection for puncture wounds through rubber-soled shoes, likely due to the organism's ability to survive in moist environments within footwear. The 3-week timeline and progression from initial wound to osteomyelitis is typical, as bone infection develops after initial soft tissue contamination. MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality for diagnosing osteomyelitis. Treatment requires prolonged courses of anti-pseudomonal antibiotics (such as fluoroquinolones or beta-lactams with anti-pseudomonal activity) and may require surgical debridement depending on extent of infection. (Choice A) Staphylococcus aureus Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of osteomyelitis overall, including hematogenous and post-traumatic osteomyelitis. However, in puncture wounds through rubber-soled shoes, Pseudomonas aeruginosa has a particular predilection and is more likely than S. aureus in this specific clinical scenario. (Choice B) Pseudomonas aeruginosa Pseudomonas aeruginosa often causes infections in puncture wounds, especially when footwear like rubber-soled shoes is involved. This pathogenicity makes it a common cause of osteomyelitis in similar cases. (Choice C) Clostridium botulinum Clostridium botulinum produces botulinum toxin causing botulism, characterized by descending flaccid paralysis. It does not cause osteomyelitis and would not present with the localized inflammatory signs seen in this case. (Choice D) Streptococcus pyogenes Streptococcus pyogenes typically causes acute soft tissue infections like cellulitis and necrotizing fasciitis. While it can occasionally cause osteomyelitis, it is much less common than other pathogens in puncture wound-associated bone infections. (Choice E) Fusobacterium necrophorum Fusobacterium necrophorum is an anaerobic organism associated with Lemierre syndrome and deep neck infections. It is not typically associated with osteomyelitis from puncture wounds, which usually involve aerobic pathogens.

question: A 28-year-old graduate student presents to the clinic with complaints of persistent, excessive worry about her academic performance, finances, and relationships for the past 9 months. She describes feeling constantly 'on edge,' with frequent headaches, difficulty falling asleep, irritability towards friends, and trouble concentrating during lectures, which has led to declining grades. She denies any specific triggers or panic attacks, and her symptoms are not limited to social situations. Physical examinations are unremarkable. Laboratory results are shown below. She has no history of substance use or other medical conditions. The diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder is made. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic treatment for this patient? WBC 6.6 x10^3/uL RBC 5.0 x10^6/uL Hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL Hematocrit 43.0 % MCV 88.0 fL MCH 30.0 pg MCHC 34.0 g/dL RDW 12.5 % Platelets 250 x10^3/uL Neutrophils 60 % Lymphocytes 30 % Monocytes 6 % Eosinophils 3 % Basophils 1 %
explanation: Explanation This patient exhibits classic features of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), including excessive worry lasting more than 6 months, accompanied by restlessness, concentration difficulties, irritability, muscle tension (manifesting as headaches), and sleep disturbances. First-line pharmacological options include selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) such as sertraline or escitalopram, or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) such as venlafaxine or duloxetine. Both drug classes have similar efficacy for GAD. Benzodiazepines are reserved for short-term use due to risks of dependence and are not recommended for long-term management. (Choice A) Venlafaxine Venlafaxine is an SNRI and a first-line pharmacological treatment for GAD, effective for both anxiety and associated symptoms with a favorable long-term profile. (Choice B) Amitriptyline Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant with efficacy for anxiety disorders but is not first-line for GAD due to its significant side effect profile, including anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention), sedation, weight gain, and potential cardiac conduction abnormalities, particularly in overdose. (Choice C) Alprazolam Alprazolam is a benzodiazepine that provides rapid symptom relief but is not recommended as first-line therapy for GAD due to significant risks of tolerance, dependence, and potentially dangerous withdrawal symptoms. Guidelines reserve benzodiazepines for short-term use or as adjunctive therapy in treatment-resistant cases. (Choice D) Quetiapine Quetiapine is an atypical antipsychotic sometimes used as adjunctive therapy for treatment-resistant anxiety disorders, but it is not first-line for GAD due to significant metabolic side effects (weight gain, diabetes risk, dyslipidemia) and sedation that outweigh benefits when effective first-line options are available. (Choice E) Propranolol Propranolol is a beta-blocker that effectively manages somatic symptoms of anxiety (palpitations, tremor) and is useful for performance anxiety, but it does not address the core cognitive symptoms of GAD such as excessive worry and rumination, making it inadequate as monotherapy for this condition.

question: A 72-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents to the ophthalmology clinic with complaints of blurred vision, eye pain, and photophobia in her left eye for the past two weeks. Three months earlier, she sustained a penetrating injury to her right eye from a fall involving broken glass, which required surgical repair and resulted in significant vision loss in that eye. She denies any recent trauma to the left eye. Ophthalmologic examination reveals bilateral granulomatous anterior uveitis, with mutton-fat keratic precipitates and posterior synechiae more pronounced in the left eye. Visual acuity is 20/200 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Explanation This presentation is most consistent with sympathetic ophthalmia, a rare bilateral granulomatous uveitis that occurs after trauma or surgery to one eye, leading to an autoimmune response against ocular antigens in both eyes, typically managed with immunosuppressive therapy to prevent vision loss. (Choice A) Lens-induced phacoanaphylactic uveitis Phacoanaphylaxis is a lens-induced granulomatous uveitis caused by autoimmune reaction to lens proteins after traumatic lens capsule rupture. While it can cause severe inflammation, it typically remains confined to the traumatized eye and does not cause the bilateral granulomatous inflammation seen in this case. (Choice B) Behçet disease Behçet disease involves recurrent oral and genital ulcers with uveitis, but it is not associated with preceding unilateral eye trauma and has a different demographic and systemic presentation. (Choice C) Sympathetic ophthalmia Sympathetic ophthalmia is an autoimmune granulomatous uveitis triggered by exposure of ocular antigens after trauma to one eye, leading to bilateral inflammation; management involves systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppressants. (Choice D) Acute post-traumatic endophthalmitis Endophthalmitis is an infectious inflammation typically following intraocular surgery or penetrating trauma. However, it usually presents acutely in the injured eye within days to weeks of trauma, not months later, and bilateral involvement without direct trauma to the second eye is extremely rare. (Choice E) Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome presents with bilateral granulomatous panuveitis but is not triggered by unilateral eye trauma. It typically includes extraocular manifestations such as sensorineural hearing loss, vitiligo, poliosis, and meningeal signs, which are absent in this case.

question: A medical school curriculum committee is reviewing the adequacy of nutrition education in their four-year MD program. A faculty member presents survey data showing that graduating medical students rate their nutrition counseling competency as low, and that practicing physicians in the United States report receiving an average of fewer than 20 hours of nutrition education during medical school — well below the minimum of 25 hours recommended by the National Academy of Sciences. A second faculty member argues that improving physician dietary habits alongside formal training would have the greatest combined impact on patient counseling outcomes. Which of the following interventions, if implemented together, would most effectively improve the quality and frequency of nutrition counseling provided by graduating physicians?

answers.label: A
answers.text: Mandating that students pass a pharmacology module covering weight-loss medications and establishing protocols to refer all dietary counseling to registered dietitians. (0%)

answers.label: B
answers.text: Focusing exclusively on student wellness programs to improve personal dietary habits without modifying the formal nutrition curriculum. (0%)

answers.label: C
answers.text: Requiring students to complete a single online nutrition module during first year and providing subsidized healthy meal options in campus dining facilities. (0%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Expanding preclinical coursework on macronutrient biochemistry and metabolic pathways without addressing practical counseling skills or student wellness initiatives. (0%)

answers.label: E
answers.text: Incorporating a minimum of 25 hours of competency-based nutrition education into the medical curriculum combined with structured self-assessment and wellness programs that help students adopt healthier personal dietary behaviors. (100%)

explanation: Explanation The majority of U.S. medical schools provide inadequate nutrition education, with most graduates receiving fewer than 20 hours — below the recommended 25-hour minimum. Evidence shows that combining formal, competency-based nutrition training with programs that encourage physicians to self-assess and improve their own dietary habits produces the greatest improvement in counseling frequency and quality. Both knowledge (education) and self-efficacy (personal modeling) are independent drivers of physician nutrition counseling behavior. (Choice A) Mandating that students pass a pharmacology module covering weight-loss medications and establishing protocols to refer all dietary counseling to registered dietitians. While knowledge of weight-loss pharmacotherapy and dietitian referrals are valuable clinical tools, this approach fails to build physician competency in nutrition counseling. Evidence demonstrates that physicians play a crucial initiating role in dietary discussions with patients. A strategy that defers all nutrition conversations to other providers reduces patient exposure to this important preventive intervention and misses opportunities for brief counseling that can occur during routine clinical encounters. (Choice B) Focusing exclusively on student wellness programs to improve personal dietary habits without modifying the formal nutrition curriculum. Improving personal dietary habits has a positive effect on counseling behavior, but without formal training in nutrition science and counseling techniques, physicians lack the knowledge base and skills needed to provide accurate and effective dietary guidance. Both elements — formal education and personal lifestyle modeling — are necessary and complementary; neither alone is sufficient to optimize counseling outcomes. (Choice C) Requiring students to complete a single online nutrition module during first year and providing subsidized healthy meal options in campus dining facilities. A single online module cannot achieve the depth and breadth of competency required for effective clinical nutrition counseling, which requires longitudinal, integrated, and skills-based training. While subsidized healthy meals provide a positive environmental influence, this intervention alone is insufficient to produce meaningful, sustained changes in dietary knowledge, counseling skills, or personal dietary behaviors needed for effective patient counseling. (Choice D) Expanding preclinical coursework on macronutrient biochemistry and metabolic pathways without addressing practical counseling skills or student wellness initiatives. Biochemical knowledge of macronutrients is foundational but does not translate directly into effective patient counseling. Practical skills such as dietary assessment, motivational interviewing, and culturally sensitive counseling are essential components that basic science instruction alone does not provide. Furthermore, ignoring the physician's personal dietary habits misses an important independent determinant of counseling behavior. (Choice E) Incorporating a minimum of 25 hours of competency-based nutrition education into the medical curriculum combined with structured self-assessment and wellness programs that help students adopt healthier personal dietary behaviors. Meeting the recommended threshold of at least 25 hours of nutrition education, as advised by the National Academy of Sciences, provides students with the foundational knowledge and counseling skills needed to discuss diet confidently with patients. Competency-based training — including practical skills like dietary history-taking and motivational interviewing around food choices — improves self-efficacy, which is a key predictor of counseling behavior. Simultaneously, structured self-assessment and physician wellness programming encourage students to reflect on and improve their own dietary habits. Research demonstrates that physicians who model healthy eating are more likely to counsel patients about nutrition and to do so with greater frequency and confidence. The synergistic effect of knowledge acquisition and personal lifestyle alignment represents the most evidence-based strategy for producing physicians who are both equipped and motivated to counsel patients on diet. This dual approach addresses the two most significant modifiable predictors of nutrition counseling behavior identified in the literature.

question: A 35-year-old Hispanic male visits the dermatology clinic for an annual check-up. During the examination, the dermatologist notices a dark, irregular lesion on his upper back.
