Targeted ultrasound demonstrates a round, well-circumscribed, anechoic lesion with posterior acoustic enhancement, consistent with a simple cyst. Fine-needle aspiration is performed, yielding 8 mL of bloody fluid, after which the mass persists on palpation. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.label: D
answers.text: Observation with follow-up ultrasound in 3 months (13.19%)

explanation: Explanation This patient has a symptomatic breast cyst that appears simple on ultrasound, but fine-needle aspiration yields bloody fluid and the mass persists. While simple breast cysts can typically be managed with fine-needle aspiration alone, bloody aspirate is a concerning feature that requires core needle biopsy to exclude underlying malignancy, regardless of benign imaging appearance. (Choice A) Core needle biopsy Core needle biopsy is indicated due to the bloody aspirate and persistent mass after aspiration, to evaluate for possible underlying malignancy. (Choice B) Repeat fine-needle aspiration Repeat aspiration is not appropriate because the bloody aspirate is a concerning feature that requires tissue sampling for histologic evaluation, not simply draining the cyst again. (Choice C) Complete surgical excision Complete surgical excision is unnecessarily invasive as the initial diagnostic step. Core needle biopsy provides adequate tissue for histologic diagnosis and should be performed first to determine if surgical excision is warranted. (Choice D) Observation with follow-up ultrasound in 3 months Observation is inappropriate when a breast cyst yields bloody aspirate on fine-needle aspiration, as this finding raises concern for malignancy and requires immediate tissue sampling with core needle biopsy. (Choice E) Bilateral mammography Mammography is not indicated as the next step because imaging has already characterized the lesion as a simple cyst, and the patient had a normal mammogram 6 months ago. The bloody aspirate requires tissue sampling, not additional imaging.

question: A 28-year-old male marathon runner presents to his primary care physician for pre-season counseling. He recently transitioned to a whole-food plant-based diet and asks about optimizing his protein intake. He currently consumes approximately 1.2 g/kg/day of protein, mostly from rice, oats, and mixed vegetables, with minimal legume intake. He trains 10–12 hours per week and reports mild fatigue and slower recovery times over the past 6 weeks. His physical exam and basic metabolic panel are unremarkable. Which of the following dietary modifications would most directly address the most likely nutritional cause of his symptoms?

answers.label: A
answers.text: Advise the patient that 1.2 g/kg/day is sufficient for endurance athletes on any dietary pattern (0%)

answers.label: B
answers.text: Increase total caloric intake by adding more grains and refined carbohydrates to his current diet (5%)

answers.label: C
answers.text: Recommend iron supplementation as the primary intervention, as plant-based diets commonly cause iron-deficiency anemia that explains his fatigue (5%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Add lysine-rich legumes such as lentils or black beans to complement grain proteins and increase total protein intake to at least 1.4–1.7 g/kg/day (90%)

answers.label: E
answers.text: Switch entirely to soy protein isolate supplements to replace all whole food protein sources (0%)

explanation: Explanation Endurance athletes require 1.4–1.7 g/kg/day of protein, and those on plant-based diets must also attend to protein quality. Rice is limiting in lysine, and a diet relying heavily on grains without legumes will have a low DIAAS, resulting in inadequate indispensable amino acid delivery despite seemingly sufficient total protein grams. Adding lysine-rich legumes (beans, lentils, soy) complements grain proteins and raises the effective amino acid score of the overall diet, supporting muscle repair and recovery. (Choice A) Advise the patient that 1.2 g/kg/day is sufficient for endurance athletes on any dietary pattern This is incorrect. Current sports nutrition guidelines from the International Society of Sports Nutrition and the American College of Sports Medicine recommend 1.4–1.7 g/kg/day for endurance athletes and up to 2.0 g/kg/day for those with significant resistance training components. An intake of 1.2 g/kg/day falls below these targets, and the issue is further compounded by low protein quality from his grain-dominant diet. (Choice B) Increase total caloric intake by adding more grains and refined carbohydrates to his current diet Increasing caloric intake via additional grains and oats would not address the underlying protein quality deficit. His current diet is already grain-predominant, and grains like rice and oats are low in lysine — the first limiting amino acid in cereals. Adding more of the same limiting protein source increases total protein grams but fails to correct the amino acid imbalance. For athletes on plant-based diets, both protein quantity AND quality must be optimized through complementary protein combinations. (Choice C) Recommend iron supplementation as the primary intervention, as plant-based diets commonly cause iron-deficiency anemia that explains his fatigue While plant-based diets can be associated with lower iron bioavailability due to non-heme iron sources, there is no laboratory evidence of anemia or iron deficiency in this case. The patient's symptoms of fatigue and impaired recovery, specifically in the context of high training volume and a grain-dominant diet lacking in lysine, are more consistent with inadequate protein quality and quantity. Iron supplementation without documented deficiency ignores the most likely nutritional cause of his symptoms. (Choice D) Add lysine-rich legumes such as lentils or black beans to complement grain proteins and increase total protein intake to at least 1.4–1.7 g/kg/day This patient's symptoms of fatigue and impaired recovery are most consistent with both insufficient total protein and poor protein quality in the context of high training volume. Endurance athletes require 1.4–1.7 g/kg/day of protein, exceeding the standard RDA of 0.8 g/kg/day; his current intake of 1.2 g/kg/day falls short. Furthermore, his diet is dominated by grains such as rice and oats, which have a low DIAAS largely due to lysine deficiency — lysine is the first limiting amino acid in most cereal grains. Legumes such as lentils, black beans, and chickpeas are rich in lysine but limiting in methionine, making them complementary to grains. By combining legumes with grains, the overall DIAAS of the diet improves substantially, providing a more complete indispensable amino acid profile. This strategy, paired with increasing total protein toward the athletic recommendation, directly addresses both dimensions of the protein adequacy problem and is the most evidence-based nutritional intervention for this scenario. (Choice E) Switch entirely to soy protein isolate supplements to replace all whole food protein sources While soy is a complete protein with a high DIAAS and would address the amino acid quality deficit, recommending replacement of all dietary protein sources with a single supplement is neither practical nor consistent with evidence-based dietary counseling. The preferred approach is to optimize whole-food dietary patterns by combining complementary plant proteins, with supplementation considered as an adjunct if total protein targets cannot be met through food alone.

question: A 28-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a 4-day history of increasing fatigue, breathlessness with minor exertion, and ankle swelling. He returned from a trip to Southeast Asia two weeks ago where he had a brief febrile illness resembling a cold. He is currently not on any medications. Vital signs reveal: temperature 37 C (98.6 F), blood pressure 115/70 mmHg, heart rate 92/min, and respiratory rate 22/min. On examination, there are bilateral basal crackles in the lungs, elevated jugular venous pressure, and bilateral 2+ pitting edema. Transthoracic echocardiogram is likely to reveal?

answers.label: A
answers.text: Reduced ejection fraction with ventricles dilatation (63.27%)

answers.label: C
answers.text: Isolated left atrial enlargement with normal ventricular function (4.08%)

answers.label: E
answers.text: Severe tricuspid valve regurgitation with normal left ventricular function (14.29%)

explanation: Explanation This patient presents with acute heart failure symptoms following a recent viral illness in Southeast Asia, consistent with post-viral dilated cardiomyopathy. The constellation of fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, bilateral crackles, elevated JVP, and peripheral edema indicates biventricular failure. Viral myocarditis can progress to dilated cardiomyopathy through direct cytotoxic effects and immune-mediated myocardial damage. The characteristic echocardiographic findings are ventricular dilation with reduced ejection fraction, reflecting systolic dysfunction that correlates with the clinical presentation of heart failure. (Choice A) Reduced ejection fraction with ventricles dilatation This is indicative of dilated cardiomyopathy, often following viral myocarditis and would perfectly match the patient's recent history and symptoms. (Choice B) Eccentric left ventricular hypertrophy Eccentric hypertrophy develops from chronic volume overload conditions (mitral regurgitation, aortic regurgitation) over months to years. The acute 4-day presentation following viral illness suggests dilated cardiomyopathy rather than chronic volume overload. (Choice C) Isolated left atrial enlargement with normal ventricular function Left atrial enlargement is a secondary finding that may accompany heart failure but doesn't explain the primary pathophysiology. Post-viral dilated cardiomyopathy presents with ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction, not isolated atrial enlargement. (Choice D) Normal echocardiogram Unlikely given the clear symptomatic presentation suggesting cardiac dysfunction. (Choice E) Severe tricuspid valve regurgitation with normal left ventricular function While tricuspid regurgitation can cause right heart failure symptoms, the bilateral crackles and acute presentation following viral illness suggest primary myocardial dysfunction rather than isolated valvular disease.

question: A 34-year-old African American woman with a long-standing history of secondary-progressive multiple sclerosis presents at the emergency department with worsening neurologic symptoms. She has experienced several exacerbations in the past, which have left her with some permanent deficits. Her previous assessment revealed coordination problems, visual disturbances, and weakness in her left arm and leg. Recent MRI findings demonstrated multiple hyperintense lesions in the left cerebral hemisphere and at the brainstem. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed oligoclonal bands. Currently, she exhibits lower limb paralysis, urinary retention, bowel incontinence, and numbness originating below her chest. Where is the new demyelinating lesion likely located?
explanation: Explanation The patient presents with paraplegia, sensory loss below the chest (nipple line corresponds to T4 dermatome), urinary retention, and bowel incontinence - a classic presentation of upper thoracic spinal cord pathology. In multiple sclerosis, demyelinating plaques can occur anywhere in the CNS, and when they involve the upper thoracic spinal cord (T1-T6 levels), they disrupt descending motor pathways causing lower limb paralysis, ascending sensory pathways causing sensory loss below the lesion level, and autonomic pathways controlling bladder and bowel function. (Choice A) Upper thoracic spinal cord Lesions in this region can cause lower limb paralysis, bladder dysfunction, and loss of sensation below the nipples. (Choice B) Cervical spinal cord Cervical spinal cord lesions would cause quadriplegia or quadriparesis affecting both upper and lower extremities, not the isolated lower limb paralysis with preserved upper limb function seen in this patient. (Choice C) Cerebellum Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria, and coordination problems, but do not cause the complete lower limb paralysis, sensory level at the chest, or autonomic dysfunction (urinary retention, bowel incontinence) seen in this patient. (Choice D) Parietal lobe Parietal lobe lesions cause cortical sensory deficits (neglect, astereognosis, agraphesthesia) and spatial processing problems, but cannot cause the complete motor paralysis, autonomic dysfunction, or dermatomal sensory level seen in this patient. (Choice E) Posterior columns Posterior column lesions cause loss of vibration sense, proprioception, and fine touch discrimination, but would not cause the motor paralysis, autonomic dysfunction, or pain/temperature sensory loss described in this patient.

question: A 72-year-old woman with a history of cerebral amyloid angiopathy presents to the emergency department after a sudden onset of severe headache, confusion, and right-sided weakness. Initial non-contrast CT head reveals a large left parietal lobe intracerebral hemorrhage with mild midline shift. Her blood pressure is 160/90 mmHg, and Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 13. She is admitted to the intensive care unit for monitoring. Two hours later, she becomes increasingly lethargic with a GCS score of 7, develops irregular respirations, and loses her gag reflex. Her left pupil is now dilated and unreactive. What is the best next step in management?

answers.label: E
answers.text: Initiate blood pressure reduction with nicardipine (0%)

explanation: Explanation This patient has an intracerebral hemorrhage likely due to cerebral amyloid angiopathy, which initially presented with focal neurologic deficits and now shows rapid deterioration due to brain herniation, leading to decreased level of consciousness and compromised airway protection. The best next step is to secure the airway with endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation to prevent asphyxiation and ensure adequate oxygenation. Further management includes blood pressure control, reversal of any coagulopathy if present, and measures to reduce intracranial pressure. (Choice A) Administer intravenous mannitol While mannitol is an osmotic diuretic used to reduce intracranial pressure in cases of herniation, it is not the immediate priority when a patient has lost protective airway reflexes and developed irregular respirations. Airway protection must always take precedence over ICP management in the ABC approach to critically ill patients. (Choice B) Obtain urgent repeat CT head While a repeat CT would likely confirm hematoma expansion or worsening herniation and could guide further management, obtaining diagnostic imaging should never delay emergent airway management in a patient with rapidly deteriorating mental status and loss of protective reflexes. (Choice C) Intubate and mechanically ventilate The patient's rapid decline in GCS, loss of gag reflex, and irregular respirations indicate brain herniation with inability to protect the airway, necessitating immediate intubation and mechanical ventilation for airway protection and to prevent respiratory arrest. (Choice D) Perform emergent decompressive craniectomy Decompressive craniectomy may be life-saving in cases of malignant cerebral edema with herniation, but surgical intervention requires a secured airway and stable patient first. The ABCs of resuscitation mandate airway protection before any operative procedure can be safely performed. (Choice E) Initiate blood pressure reduction with nicardipine Blood pressure reduction with agents like nicardipine is important in intracerebral hemorrhage to prevent hematoma expansion (target <140 mmHg systolic), but securing the airway takes absolute priority when the patient shows signs of impending respiratory failure and inability to protect their airway.

question: A 60-year-old postmenopausal woman with a history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension presents for evaluation after experiencing a vertebral compression fracture from a low-impact fall. Her dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan reveals a T-score of -3.1 at the lumbar spine and -2.6 at the femoral neck. She reports a sedentary lifestyle and inadequate dietary calcium intake. In addition to recommending weight-bearing exercises, smoking cessation if applicable, and supplementation with calcium and vitamin D, which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacologic therapy?
explanation: Explanation This patient has postmenopausal osteoporosis confirmed by DEXA scan and a fragility fracture. Initial management includes lifestyle modifications and calcium/vitamin D supplementation. Bisphosphonates, such as oral alendronate, are the first-line pharmacologic treatment for most women with postmenopausal osteoporosis. (Choice A) Subcutaneous teriparatide Teriparatide is an anabolic PTH analog reserved for patients with severe osteoporosis (T-score ≤-3.5, multiple fractures, or fractures on bisphosphonate therapy) due to its high cost, daily injection requirement, and potential side effects. It stimulates bone formation rather than just preventing bone loss, making it valuable in very high-risk patients. (Choice B) Subcutaneous denosumab Denosumab is a second-line option typically reserved for patients who cannot tolerate bisphosphonates due to GI side effects, have contraindications such as severe renal impairment (eGFR <35), or have failed bisphosphonate therapy. While effective, it is not first-line due to higher cost and potential for rebound bone loss if discontinued. (Choice C) Intranasal calcitonin Calcitonin has modest anti-fracture efficacy and is primarily used for short-term management of acute vertebral compression fracture pain due to its analgesic properties. It is not recommended as first-line therapy for osteoporosis prevention due to limited fracture reduction data and concerns about potential increased malignancy risk with long-term use. (Choice D) Oral alendronate Bisphosphonates like alendronate are first-line therapy for postmenopausal osteoporosis due to their efficacy in reducing fracture risk by inhibiting bone resorption. (Choice E) Oral raloxifene Raloxifene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that reduces vertebral fracture risk but has no proven efficacy for hip fractures. It is typically reserved for postmenopausal women at high risk for breast cancer who also have osteoporosis, or as an alternative when bisphosphonates are contraindicated or not tolerated.

question: A 25-year-old soccer player is brought to the clinic by his coach due to a painful, swollen right knee following a twisting injury during a match. He noted a popping sensation at the time of the injury, followed by immediate swelling. Physical assessment reveals a tender, swollen knee with instability to varus stress. A varus stress test causes pronounced lateral joint laxity. What is the most appropriate imaging study to confirm the diagnosis of a lateral collateral ligament injury?

answers.label: C
answers.text: CT scan of the knee joint (1.32%)

explanation: Explanation This scenario describes a lateral collateral ligament (LCL) injury following a varus stress mechanism. The LCL provides lateral knee stability and resists varus angulation. A twisting injury with immediate swelling, popping sensation, and positive varus stress test strongly suggests LCL tear. MRI is the gold standard for evaluating suspected ligament injuries, providing excellent soft tissue contrast to assess tear severity, concurrent meniscal damage, and other associated injuries. It is non-invasive and more comprehensive than physical examination alone for surgical planning. (Choice A) Arthroscopy of the knee joint Arthroscopy is an invasive surgical procedure that allows direct visualization and potential treatment of intra-articular structures. However, it is typically reserved for cases where MRI is inconclusive or when therapeutic intervention is planned simultaneously with diagnosis. It carries surgical risks and is not first-line for diagnostic purposes. (Choice B) Bone Scan Bone scans are generally used to detect stress fractures, osteomyelitis, or metastatic bone disease, not soft tissue injuries. (Choice C) CT scan of the knee joint CT scans excel at detecting bony injuries, fractures, and joint effusions but provide poor soft tissue contrast. Ligaments, tendons, and cartilage are not well-differentiated on CT imaging, making it inadequate for diagnosing lateral collateral ligament tears. (Choice D) MRI of the knee joint MRI is the best modality for visualizing soft tissue injuries like ligament tears, including the lateral collateral ligament. (Choice E) Ultrasound of the knee joint While ultrasound can visualize superficial structures and has some utility for ACL assessment, it is operator-dependent and provides limited visualization of the lateral collateral ligament compared to MRI. Dynamic ultrasound can show ligament laxity but lacks the comprehensive soft tissue detail needed for complete evaluation.

question: A 19-month-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic by his parents, who are concerned that he is not walking yet. He was exclusively breastfed until 14 months and has been a selective eater since. He lives in a northern city and has minimal outdoor sun exposure. On examination, he has bowing of both lower extremities, widening of the wrists, and palpable enlargement of the costochondral junctions bilaterally. His anterior fontanelle remains open. Laboratory studies show calcium 8.0 mg/dL, phosphorus 2.6 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 680 U/L, PTH 142 pg/mL, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 11 ng/mL. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of this child's skeletal findings?

answers.label: A
answers.text: Primary hypoparathyroidism causing inadequate PTH secretion and hypocalcemia (0%)

answers.label: B
answers.text: Vitamin D deficiency impairing intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, causing secondary hyperparathyroidism and defective bone mineralization at growth plates (0%)

answers.label: C
answers.text: Dietary calcium deficiency from inadequate calcium intake during exclusive breastfeeding (100%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets causing renal phosphate wasting through FGF23 excess (0%)

answers.label: E
answers.text: Copper deficiency causing impaired lysyl oxidase activity and defective collagen synthesis (0%)

explanation: Explanation This child has nutritional rickets from vitamin D deficiency. Low vitamin D impairs intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, causing hypocalcemia and hypophosphatemia. Secondary hyperparathyroidism maintains serum calcium at the expense of bone resorption, while inadequate calcium-phosphate product leads to defective bone mineralization, widened growth plates, and skeletal deformity. (Choice A) Primary hypoparathyroidism causing inadequate PTH secretion and hypocalcemia Primary hypoparathyroidism would cause hypocalcemia with low, not elevated, PTH levels. This child has secondary hyperparathyroidism (elevated PTH at 142 pg/mL) as a compensatory response to vitamin D deficiency-induced hypocalcemia. Primary hypoparathyroidism would not explain the skeletal deformities of rickets. (Choice B) Vitamin D deficiency impairing intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, causing secondary hyperparathyroidism and defective bone mineralization at growth plates This child has nutritional rickets caused by vitamin D deficiency. Vitamin D is required for expression of intestinal calcium transport proteins and renal phosphate reabsorption. Deficiency causes hypocalcemia and hypophosphatemia, stimulating secondary hyperparathyroidism (PTH 142 pg/mL). While PTH partially restores serum calcium through bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption, the reduced calcium-phosphate product is insufficient for normal osteoid mineralization. This causes accumulation of unmineralized osteoid at growth plates, resulting in widened, frayed metaphyses, rachitic rosary at costochondral junctions, craniotabes, and bowing of weight-bearing bones. Elevated alkaline phosphatase reflects increased osteoblast activity attempting to compensate. Treatment is vitamin D and calcium supplementation. (Choice C) Dietary calcium deficiency from inadequate calcium intake during exclusive breastfeeding While dietary calcium deficiency can contribute to rickets, this child's presentation is primarily driven by vitamin D deficiency, evidenced by the very low 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of 11 ng/mL. The clinical context of exclusive breastfeeding with minimal sun exposure in a northern city points to inadequate vitamin D synthesis and intake. Dietary calcium deficiency alone would not typically cause such severe secondary hyperparathyroidism or explain the low vitamin D level. (Choice D) Hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets causing renal phosphate wasting through FGF23 excess X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH) typically presents with isolated hypophosphatemia, normal calcium levels, and normal or low-normal PTH. Patients with XLH have normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels, unlike this patient who has a severely deficient level of 11 ng/mL. The combination of hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, elevated PTH, and very low vitamin D confirms nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets rather than a hereditary phosphate-wasting disorder. (Choice E) Copper deficiency causing impaired lysyl oxidase activity and defective collagen synthesis Copper deficiency causes impaired collagen and elastin cross-linking due to reduced lysyl oxidase activity and can cause metaphyseal changes on radiograph, but it does not explain hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism, or a 25-hydroxyvitamin D of 11 ng/mL. The laboratory profile and clinical context of minimal sun exposure and exclusive breastfeeding are diagnostic of vitamin D deficiency rickets.

question: A 32-year-old G1P0 woman at 8 weeks' gestation by last menstrual period presents to her obstetrician for a follow-up visit after a recent international trip. She reports that her initial pregnancy symptoms, such as breast tenderness and mild nausea, have resolved over the past week, but she denies any vaginal bleeding, cramping, or abdominal pain. Her medical history is unremarkable, and she takes no medications. On examination, her vital signs are normal, and the cervix is closed with no blood in the vaginal vault. Serum β-hCG level is 12,000 mIU/mL, which is lower than her level of 18,000 mIU/mL measured 5 days ago. Transvaginal ultrasound reveals an intrauterine gestational sac measuring 8 weeks in size with a yolk sac but no fetal pole or cardiac activity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Explanation The patient's resolution of pregnancy symptoms, closed cervix, decreasing β-hCG levels, and ultrasound findings of an intrauterine gestational sac with a yolk sac but without a fetal pole or cardiac activity are consistent with a missed abortion. This differs from an ectopic pregnancy (typically extrauterine location), hydatidiform mole (grape-like vesicles on ultrasound), incomplete abortion (open cervix with passage of tissue), threatened abortion (viable pregnancy with bleeding), or normal pregnancy (expected fetal development and rising β-hCG). (Choice A) Normal pregnancy A normal pregnancy at 8 weeks would show rising β-hCG levels, presence of a fetal pole with cardiac activity on ultrasound, and continuation of symptoms, not the findings described. (Choice B) Complete hydatidiform mole Complete hydatidiform mole presents with markedly elevated β-hCG levels (often >100,000 mIU/mL), vaginal bleeding with passage of grape-like vesicles, and ultrasound showing a characteristic 'snowstorm' appearance. The β-hCG level here is relatively modest and decreasing. (Choice C) Ectopic pregnancy Ectopic pregnancy typically presents with abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and β-hCG levels that rise slower than expected or plateau. The presence of an intrauterine gestational sac with yolk sac definitively rules out ectopic pregnancy. (Choice D) Missed abortion Missed abortion is characterized by fetal demise without expulsion, presenting with loss of symptoms, closed cervix, decreasing β-hCG, and ultrasound showing a nonviable intrauterine pregnancy, matching this case. (Choice E) Incomplete abortion Incomplete abortion involves an open cervix with partial passage of products of conception, often with heavy bleeding and cramping, unlike this patient's closed cervix and lack of symptoms.

question: A 62-year-old female presents with increasing facial puffiness and swelling around the eyes, predominantly in the mornings. She has noticed mild breathlessness during physical activities and has unintentionally lost 8 pounds over the last two months. Her medical history includes chronic painful joints due to osteoarthritis, for which she takes over-the-counter NSAIDs. She has a 30-year history of tobacco use. During examination, there is facial congestion and cyanosis, alongside engorged neck and chest wall veins. Abdominal examination is unremarkable; no edema in the lower limbs is noted. What is the most appropriate initial investigation in the management of this patient?
explanation: Explanation This patient presents with classic superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome: facial puffiness, periorbital swelling worse in mornings, facial cyanosis, and neck vein engorgement. The smoking history and unintentional weight loss raise concern for thoracic malignancy as the underlying cause. Chest x-ray is the appropriate initial investigation, identifying mediastinal abnormalities in over 80% of SVC syndrome cases and guiding further management decisions. (Choice A) Chest x-ray Chest x-ray is the appropriate initial investigation for suspected superior vena cava syndrome. It can identify mediastinal masses, widening, or other thoracic abnormalities in over 80% of SVC syndrome cases. Given this patient's smoking history, weight loss, and classic SVC syndrome presentation, chest x-ray will help identify potential malignancies causing venous obstruction and guide further imaging decisions. (Choice B) CT angiography of the head CT angiography of the head evaluates intracranial vascular pathology such as aneurysms or stroke. This patient's presentation of facial puffiness, neck vein engorgement, and upper body congestion indicates superior vena cava syndrome, which requires thoracic rather than cranial imaging to identify mediastinal causes. (Choice C) Doppler ultrasound of the neck While Doppler ultrasound of the neck can assess venous flow patterns, it has limited utility in superior vena cava syndrome. The obstruction typically occurs at the mediastinal level where the SVC is compressed by masses, making neck Doppler insufficient to identify the underlying cause or extent of obstruction. (Choice D) Echocardiogram Echocardiogram assesses cardiac structure and function but would not identify the cause of superior vena cava syndrome. While heart failure can cause facial swelling, this patient's pattern of upper body venous congestion without lower extremity edema, combined with smoking history and weight loss, points to mechanical SVC obstruction rather than cardiac dysfunction. (Choice E) Carotid artery ultrasound Carotid ultrasound evaluates carotid artery stenosis and cerebrovascular disease. While this patient has facial swelling and neck vein engorgement, these findings combined with the clinical context (smoking history, weight loss, upper body venous congestion) suggest superior vena cava syndrome rather than cerebrovascular pathology.

question: A 68-year-old woman with a history of metastatic colon cancer is undergoing chemotherapy. She presents to the emergency department with acute right leg swelling and pain. Doppler ultrasound confirms an extensive deep venous thrombosis in the right femoral and popliteal veins. Her lab values are shown below, and she has a history of severe gastrointestinal bleeding from her tumor one week ago, precluding anticoagulation. Vital signs are stable, and she has no signs of pulmonary embolism. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? WBC 7.2 x10^3/μL Neutrophils 60% Lymphocytes 30% Monocytes 6% Eosinophils 3% Basophils 1% RBC 4.8 x10^6/μL Hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL Hematocrit 42% MCV 90 fL MCH 29.5 pg MCHC 33.8 g/dL RDW 12.8% Platelets 45000/mm³ MPV 10.0 fL

answers.label: A
answers.text: Place a retrievable inferior vena cava filter (98.63%)

answers.label: B
answers.text: Initiate low-molecular-weight heparin at prophylactic dose (1.37%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Apply graduated compression stockings and monitor (0%)

explanation: Explanation This patient with metastatic cancer has a proximal deep venous thrombosis but contraindications to anticoagulation due to thrombocytopenia and recent severe bleeding. Placement of a retrievable inferior vena cava filter is indicated to prevent pulmonary embolism while avoiding bleeding risks. Other options like anticoagulation are contraindicated, and alternatives such as compression stockings or observation are insufficient for preventing embolization in this high-risk scenario. (Choice A) Place a retrievable inferior vena cava filter This is correct. An IVC filter is indicated to prevent pulmonary embolism in patients with proximal DVT and contraindications to anticoagulation. (Choice B) Initiate low-molecular-weight heparin at prophylactic dose This is incorrect. While LMWH is typically first-line for DVT treatment, it is contraindicated here due to severe thrombocytopenia (platelets 45,000) and recent severe gastrointestinal bleeding, both of which significantly increase hemorrhage risk. (Choice C) Initiate warfarin with heparin bridge This is incorrect due to the contraindication to anticoagulation from thrombocytopenia and recent bleeding. (Choice D) Apply graduated compression stockings and monitor This is incorrect. While compression stockings provide symptomatic relief and may reduce post-thrombotic syndrome, they do not prevent pulmonary embolism in patients with proximal DVT. Given the high embolic risk from femoral and popliteal clots, mechanical prophylaxis alone is inadequate. (Choice E) Observation with serial ultrasounds This is incorrect. Observation alone carries unacceptable risk of pulmonary embolism in patients with proximal DVT, particularly femoral and popliteal involvement which have high embolic potential. Without anticoagulation or mechanical protection, PE risk approaches 50%.

question: A 28-year-old otherwise healthy man presents to the clinic with a 3-day history of high fever, chills, productive cough with rusty sputum, and pleuritic chest pain on the left side. He reports no recent travel, sick contacts, or underlying lung disease. Vital signs show temperature 39.2°C (102.6°F), heart rate 110/min, respiratory rate 24/min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Physical examination reveals decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the left lower lung field. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.label: B
answers.text: Symptomatic treatment with antipyretics and fluids only (0%)

explanation: Invert Contrast Zoom

question: A 32-year-old respiratory therapist presents with a 3-day history of pain and swelling on her right index finger. She reports low-grade fever, fatigue, and mild headache. She frequently intubates patients in the intensive care unit and recalls a small cut on her finger from two weeks ago while handling orotracheal secretions from a patient with known oral herpes lesions. The examination findings and lab values are shown below. She denies any genital symptoms or recent sexual activity. This patient's condition is most likely caused by which of the following? WBC Count 7200 /µL Neutrophils 48 % Lymphocytes 45 % Monocytes 5 % Eosinophils 1 % Basophils 1 % Hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL Hematocrit 42 % RBC Count 4.8 million/µL Platelet Count 250000 /µL
explanation: Explanation This respiratory therapist with exposure to orotracheal secretions has systemic symptoms and a localized vesicular lesion on her finger consistent with herpetic whitlow due to herpes simplex virus inoculation through a cutaneous defect. Symptoms include fever, malaise, and grouped vesicles on an erythematous base. Recurrences are common. β-Hemolytic streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus typically cause cellulitis or abscesses without prominent vesicles. Coxsackievirus causes hand-foot-and-mouth disease with oral and bilateral extremity involvement. Disseminated gonococcal infection presents with multiple, painless pustules. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is associated with hot tub folliculitis or wound infections but not isolated vesicular eruptions. Rocky Mountain spotted fever features a centrifugal petechial rash. Secondary syphilis has a symmetric maculopapular rash often involving palms and soles. Trichophyton species cause dermatophytosis with scaly, annular plaques rather than vesicles. Varicella-zoster virus causes shingles with dermatomal distribution, not isolated finger involvement. (Choice A) Herpes simplex virus Herpes simplex virus causes herpetic whitlow through inoculation of skin breaks, leading to painful vesicular lesions on the hand with systemic symptoms; this matches the exposure history and presentation. (Choice B) Neisseria gonorrhoeae Disseminated gonococcal infection presents with multiple painless pustules, arthralgias, and tenosynovitis, not a solitary vesicular cluster. (Choice C) Pseudomonas aeruginosa Pseudomonas causes folliculitis or cellulitis post-exposure (e.g., hot tubs), but not focal vesicular eruptions on a single finger. (Choice D) Rickettsia rickettsii Rickettsia rickettsii causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever with a diffuse macular rash progressing to petechiae, starting on extremities but not localized to one finger. (Choice E) Staphylococcus aureus Staphylococcus aureus typically causes purulent skin and soft tissue infections such as furuncles, carbuncles, or abscesses, but does not produce the characteristic grouped vesicles seen in herpetic whitlow.

question: A 29-year-old African American woman presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of sharp chest pain and difficulty breathing shortly after a long-haul flight from Europe. The pain is worse when she breathes deeply or coughs. She experienced mild coughing but denies any fever or night sweats. She is a non-smoker, drinks alcohol socially, and is currently using oral contraceptives. Her uncle passed away from a stroke at age 59. Vital signs are: temperature of 37.0°C (98.6°F), heart rate of 112/min, respiratory rate of 22/min, and blood pressure of 118/72 mmHg. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her chest pain.
explanation: Invert Contrast Zoom

question: A 55-year-old man with a history of extensive small bowel resection due to complications from long-standing Crohn disease presents with chronic diarrhea, irritability, confusion, and a pruritic, hyperpigmented rash on his neck, dorsal hands, and forearms. The rash has well-demarcated borders and worsens after sun exposure. He reports a diet limited to easily digestible foods but admits to poor adherence to nutritional supplements. Physical examination finding is shown below. Which of the following vitamin deficiencies is most likely responsible for this patient's symptoms?
explanation: Explanation This patient with malabsorption secondary to extensive small bowel resection from Crohn disease presents with pellagra due to niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency. Pellagra classically presents with the 4 Ds: diarrhea, dermatitis (photosensitive rash with hyperpigmentation and well-demarcated borders), dementia (manifesting as irritability and confusion), and potentially death if untreated. The image shows glossitis, which commonly accompanies pellagra and other B-vitamin deficiencies in malabsorptive states. (Choice A) Riboflavin Riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency causes ariboflavinosis with characteristic oral and ocular manifestations including angular cheilitis, glossitis, and corneal vascularization. Unlike pellagra, riboflavin deficiency does not produce photosensitive skin lesions or the neuropsychiatric symptoms of irritability and confusion. (Choice B) Ascorbic acid Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) deficiency causes scurvy, characterized by bleeding tendencies (petechiae, ecchymoses, gingival bleeding), impaired wound healing, and fatigue due to defective collagen synthesis. Scurvy does not produce the photosensitive hyperpigmented dermatitis or neuropsychiatric manifestations seen in this patient with pellagra. (Choice C) Niacin Niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency causes pellagra, presenting with the 4 Ds: diarrhea, photosensitive dermatitis, dementia/depression, and death if untreated. This is common in malabsorptive states like post-resection Crohn disease. (Choice D) Thiamine Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency causes beriberi with peripheral neuropathy and heart failure (wet beriberi) or Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome with encephalopathy and memory issues. While confusion can occur, thiamine deficiency does not cause the characteristic photosensitive dermatitis with hyperpigmentation or the specific tetrad of symptoms seen in pellagra. (Choice E) Pyridoxine Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency primarily causes peripheral neuropathy, sideroblastic anemia, and in severe cases, seizures or depression. However, it does not cause the pathognomonic photosensitive dermatitis with well-demarcated hyperpigmented borders or the gastrointestinal symptoms characteristic of pellagra.

question: A 45-year-old woman presents to her physician with complaints of excessive daytime sleepiness, frequent headaches upon waking, and difficulty staying alert during her job as a librarian. Her partner reports that she snores loudly at night and has episodes where she appears to gasp for air, followed by brief awakenings. She denies chest pain or shortness of breath during the day. Her medical history includes hypothyroidism, treated with levothyroxine, and she has a body mass index of 28 kg/m². Physical examination shows a short neck and enlarged tonsils. Polysomnography is planned. What is the most likely mechanism causing this patient's nocturnal symptoms?

answers.label: A
answers.text: Absent respiratory drive from central nervous system dysfunction (5.8%)

answers.label: C
answers.text: Nocturnal acid reflux causing airway irritation (0%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Inflammatory lung disease causing nocturnal hypoxemia (0%)

explanation: Explanation This patient with daytime sleepiness, morning headaches, snoring, and witnessed gasping likely has obstructive sleep apnea due to intermittent collapse of the upper airway from pharyngeal muscle relaxation during sleep. Supporting features include enlarged tonsils and anatomical factors predisposing to airway obstruction, unrelated to her treated hypothyroidism. (Choice A) Absent respiratory drive from central nervous system dysfunction Central sleep apnea involves absent or reduced respiratory effort due to failure of central nervous system respiratory drive. This patient's loud snoring and witnessed gasping episodes are characteristic of obstructive rather than central sleep apnea, where airway obstruction (not absent respiratory effort) is the primary mechanism. (Choice B) Intermittent upper airway collapse This is the primary mechanism of obstructive sleep apnea, where relaxation of pharyngeal muscles during sleep leads to transient obstruction, causing hypoventilation, arousals, and symptoms like snoring and gasping. (Choice C) Nocturnal acid reflux causing airway irritation While gastroesophageal reflux can cause nocturnal coughing, choking, or throat clearing, it does not typically cause the loud snoring and witnessed apneic episodes described. GERD-related sleep disturbance usually presents with heartburn, regurgitation, or chronic cough rather than the classic triad of snoring, witnessed apneas, and excessive daytime sleepiness. (Choice D) Inflammatory lung disease causing nocturnal hypoxemia Conditions like interstitial lung disease cause dyspnea and hypoxia but not the episodic nocturnal choking with snoring seen here. (Choice E) Cardiac arrhythmia-induced arousals Cardiac arrhythmias can cause nocturnal awakenings and potentially contribute to sleep fragmentation, but they do not cause loud snoring or witnessed gasping episodes. Additionally, this patient lacks other cardiac symptoms such as palpitations, chest pain, or dyspnea that would suggest an underlying arrhythmia.

question: A 40-year-old woman is experiencing persistent right flank pain described as "sharp" and "intense." The pain worsens at night and has been ongoing for two days. She has a history of nausea and has vomited once. Her appetite has decreased, but she denies any urinary frequency or burning sensation during urination. She's otherwise healthy, with no fever. On examination, the patient's mucous membranes are slightly dry, and her heart and lungs are within normal limits. Her abdomen is soft but tender upon palpation at the right flank region. A detailed examination of the pelvis indicates no abnormalities. Which diagnostic test is most appropriate for this clinical scenario?

answers.label: A
answers.text: Proceed with surgery as scheduled and initiate total parenteral nutrition postoperatively

answers.label: B
answers.text: Administer intravenous albumin infusions preoperatively to correct hypoalbuminemia before surgery

answers.label: C
answers.text: Refer the patient to physical therapy only and proceed with surgery as scheduled

answers.label: D
answers.text: Delay surgery 7–14 days and initiate enteral nutritional supplementation to optimize preoperative nutritional status

answers.label: E
answers.text: Proceed with surgery as scheduled and advance diet postoperatively from clear liquids to regular diet as tolerated

explanation: Explanation This patient presents with classic renal colic: severe unilateral flank pain, nausea, and costovertebral angle tenderness. Non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the diagnostic test of choice for suspected nephrolithiasis, offering superior sensitivity and specificity compared to other modalities. It accurately identifies stone presence, size, location, and degree of obstruction, providing essential information for treatment planning. While urinalysis and ultrasound may provide supportive information, CT remains the gold standard for definitive diagnosis. (Choice A) Pelvic ultrasound While ultrasound can detect hydronephrosis and larger stones in the kidney, it has poor sensitivity for ureteral stones and cannot reliably exclude urolithiasis. It may miss stones that cause significant symptoms, making it inadequate as the primary diagnostic test in this clinical scenario. (Choice B) Non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis Non-contrast CT scan is the gold standard for diagnosing kidney stones, with excellent sensitivity (>95%) for detecting stones of all compositions. It provides precise information about stone size, location, and degree of obstruction, which is crucial for determining treatment approach. (Choice C) Abdominal MRI MRI is not typically used for detecting kidney stones due to its lower sensitivity. CT remains the standard for confirming stones. (Choice D) Urinalysis Urinalysis is a supportive test that may show microscopic hematuria in kidney stone patients, but hematuria is absent in 10-15% of cases. It cannot confirm the presence, size, or location of stones, which are essential for management decisions. Urinalysis alone would miss the diagnosis in this symptomatic patient.

question: A 67-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes and peripheral vascular disease is scheduled to undergo an elective left below-knee amputation in 3 weeks. He reports a 12-pound unintentional weight loss over the past 3 months and has had poor oral intake due to chronic wound pain. On exam, he appears cachectic with temporal wasting and bilateral lower extremity edema. His BMI is 17.8 kg/m². Laboratory studies show albumin 2.1 g/dL, prealbumin 9 mg/dL, and total lymphocyte count 900/mm³. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in perioperative nutritional management for this patient?

answers.label: A
answers.text: Proceed with surgery as scheduled and initiate total parenteral nutrition postoperatively (0%)

answers.label: B
answers.text: Administer intravenous albumin infusions preoperatively to correct hypoalbuminemia before surgery (0%)

answers.label: C
answers.text: Refer the patient to physical therapy only and proceed with surgery as scheduled (0%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Delay surgery 7–14 days and initiate enteral nutritional supplementation to optimize preoperative nutritional status (85.71%)

answers.label: E
answers.text: Proceed with surgery as scheduled and advance diet postoperatively from clear liquids to regular diet as tolerated (14.29%)

explanation: Explanation Severely malnourished surgical patients identified preoperatively should receive 7–14 days of nutritional optimization prior to elective surgery to reduce postoperative complications such as poor wound healing, infection, and anastomotic breakdown. Objective markers of malnutrition include BMI <18.5, unintentional weight loss >10% over 6 months, albumin <3.0 g/dL, and prealbumin <15 mg/dL. Delaying elective surgery to optimize nutrition is appropriate when the risk of malnutrition-related complications outweighs the risk of delay. (Choice A) Proceed with surgery as scheduled and initiate total parenteral nutrition postoperatively While TPN can support nutritional needs postoperatively, initiating it without first attempting preoperative optimization in a severely malnourished patient misses an opportunity to reduce surgical risk. Moreover, enteral nutrition is preferred over parenteral nutrition whenever the gut is functional, as it preserves mucosal integrity, reduces infectious complications, and is more physiologically appropriate. Proceeding with elective surgery in a severely malnourished patient without optimization significantly increases the risk of wound dehiscence, infection, and prolonged recovery. (Choice B) Administer intravenous albumin infusions preoperatively to correct hypoalbuminemia before surgery Exogenous albumin infusion does not address the underlying protein-calorie malnutrition or improve surgical outcomes. Albumin has a half-life of approximately 21 days and redistributes rapidly from the intravascular space, making serum levels a poor indicator of nutritional repletion. Current evidence-based guidelines do not support albumin infusion for preoperative nutritional optimization, as it fails to correct the functional nutritional deficits that increase surgical complications. (Choice C) Refer the patient to physical therapy only and proceed with surgery as scheduled Physical therapy is an important component of perioperative rehabilitation and prehabilitation programs, but it does not address this patient's severe nutritional deficiency that poses a direct and significant threat to wound healing and surgical outcomes. Proceeding with elective surgery in the setting of severe malnutrition without nutritional optimization contradicts established perioperative care guidelines. Physical therapy alone cannot compensate for the metabolic deficits present in severe protein-calorie malnutrition. (Choice D) Delay surgery 7–14 days and initiate enteral nutritional supplementation to optimize preoperative nutritional status This patient demonstrates severe protein-calorie malnutrition based on multiple objective criteria: BMI 17.8 kg/m², >10% unintentional weight loss over 3 months, albumin 2.1 g/dL, and prealbumin 9 mg/dL. Current evidence-based guidelines (ERAS Society, ASPEN) recommend delaying elective surgery by 7–14 days in severely malnourished patients to allow nutritional repletion, as this significantly reduces postoperative complication rates including wound dehiscence, infection, and anastomotic failure. Enteral supplementation is preferred over parenteral nutrition when the gastrointestinal tract is functional, as it maintains gut mucosal integrity, supports the immune system, and is associated with fewer infectious complications. High-protein oral nutritional supplements (targeting 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day of protein) should be initiated immediately. For elective amputation specifically, adequate preoperative nutrition also improves stump healing, which is critical for prosthetic fitting and long-term rehabilitation outcomes. Nutritional optimization in this window represents one of the highest-yield preoperative interventions available. (Choice E) Proceed with surgery as scheduled and advance diet postoperatively from clear liquids to regular diet as tolerated This approach fails to address the severe preoperative malnutrition that significantly increases surgical risk. While advancing diet postoperatively is generally appropriate, this patient's objective markers of severe malnutrition (BMI 17.8, albumin 2.1 g/dL, 12-pound weight loss) require preoperative optimization. Relying solely on postoperative dietary advancement in a severely malnourished patient substantially increases the risk of wound dehiscence, infection, and poor healing outcomes.

question: A 74-year-old woman presents with six months of progressively worsening coordination issues along with occasional urinary accidents. She reports no significant changes in urine frequency or discomfort, and denies any recent consistent headaches. Her medical history includes treated hypertension and early-stage breast cancer from five years ago. On examination, she shows stable vital signs. Heart and pulmonary assessments are normal, and neither cranial nor motor deficits are noted. However, her gait is notably unstable and slow, characterized by short steps. She scores 23/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Muscle strength is intact, and reflexes are without abnormality. What is the most likely cause of her current symptoms?
explanation: Explanation This patient presents with the classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH): progressive gait abnormalities (magnetic gait with short steps), urinary incontinence without urgency, and mild cognitive decline (MoCA 23/30). NPH results from impaired CSF absorption, leading to communicating hydrocephalus with ventricular enlargement but normal opening pressures. Early recognition is crucial as NPH is one of the few reversible causes of dementia, with surgical intervention (ventriculoperitoneal shunt) often improving symptoms significantly. (Choice A) Intracellular neurofibrillary tangles Neurofibrillary tangles are the hallmark pathology of Alzheimer's disease, which typically presents with progressive memory loss as the predominant early symptom, rather than the gait-predominant presentation with preserved strength and reflexes seen in this patient. (Choice B) Degenerative cervical myelopathy Degenerative cervical myelopathy typically presents with upper motor neuron signs including hyperreflexia, spasticity, and pathological reflexes (Hoffman's sign, Babinski), none of which are present in this patient with normal reflexes and strength. (Choice C) Reduced CSF absorption In normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH), reduced CSF absorption leads to ventricular enlargement, resulting in gait abnormality, urinary incontinence, and cognitive decline. (Choice D) Cerebral small vessel disease While cerebral small vessel disease can cause gait instability and cognitive decline, it typically presents with more prominent cognitive symptoms and focal neurological deficits, rather than the classic triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and mild cognitive impairment seen in NPH. (Choice E) Overproduction of cerebrospinal fluid Overproduction of CSF (choroid plexus papilloma) is extremely rare and typically presents with signs of increased intracranial pressure, not the normal-pressure pattern seen in this patient with classic NPH triad.

question: A global health physician is designing a nutritional supplementation program for children aged 6–59 months in a sub-Saharan African community with high rates of acute lower respiratory tract infections and diarrheal disease. Local dietary surveys reveal widespread deficiencies in multiple micronutrients. The physician reviews evidence-based guidelines for reducing infectious disease morbidity and mortality in this population. Which of the following combinations of micronutrient supplementation strategies is best supported by evidence for reducing infection-related mortality in this pediatric population?

answers.label: A
answers.text: Iodine and selenium supplementation to optimize thyroid function and antioxidant enzyme activity (0%)

answers.label: B
answers.text: Iron and folate supplementation to prevent anemia and support hematopoiesis (40%)

answers.label: C
answers.text: Calcium and phosphorus supplementation to support bone mineralization and prevent rickets-related respiratory compromise (0%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Vitamin A supplementation and zinc supplementation targeting diarrheal and respiratory infections (60%)

answers.label: E
answers.text: High-dose vitamin C and vitamin E supplementation to reduce oxidative stress during acute infections (0%)

explanation: Invert Contrast Zoom

question: A 72-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease presents to the emergency department with substernal chest pain radiating to his left arm, which began 4 hours ago while he was gardening. Electrocardiography is shown. Serum troponin levels are elevated. Coronary angiography reveals a 90% stenosis in the right coronary artery, and he undergoes percutaneous coronary intervention with placement of a drug-eluting stent. He is started on aspirin therapy. Which of the following medications should be added to his regimen for at least 12 months to reduce the risk of recurrent myocardial infarction and stent thrombosis?
explanation: Explanation This patient has experienced a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and received a drug-eluting stent. Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and a P2Y12 receptor blocker is recommended for at least 12 months to prevent recurrent cardiovascular events and stent thrombosis. (Choice A) Direct oral anticoagulant Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) like rivaroxaban may be considered in select post-MI patients with additional indications such as atrial fibrillation, typically as triple therapy with dual antiplatelet agents. However, they do not replace P2Y12 inhibitors in dual antiplatelet therapy as they target different pathways (coagulation vs platelet aggregation). (Choice B) Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors are potent antiplatelet agents used peri-procedurally during high-risk PCI but are not recommended for long-term outpatient dual antiplatelet therapy due to increased bleeding risk without proven long-term benefit compared to P2Y12 inhibitors. (Choice C) Vitamin K antagonist Vitamin K antagonists like warfarin are anticoagulants that prevent thromboembolism in conditions such as atrial fibrillation or venous thromboembolism. They do not provide the specific antiplatelet effects needed to prevent arterial thrombosis and stent thrombosis in post-MI patients. (Choice D) Proton pump inhibitor Proton pump inhibitors may be used to reduce gastrointestinal bleeding risk in patients on dual antiplatelet therapy, but they are not antiplatelet agents and do not directly prevent recurrent MI or stent thrombosis. (Choice E) P2Y12 receptor blocker P2Y12 receptor blockers, such as clopidogrel, prasugrel, or ticagrelor, are recommended in combination with aspirin for dual antiplatelet therapy to reduce recurrent MI, cardiovascular death, and stent thrombosis in patients post-NSTEMI with drug-eluting stent placement.

question: A 65-year-old man with a history of prosthetic aortic valve replacement 5 years ago presents with 3 weeks of intermittent fevers, night sweats, and fatigue. Physical examination shows a temperature of 38.5°C (101.3°F), a new aortic regurgitant murmur, Janeway lesions on the palms, and tender splenomegaly. Laboratory studies are shown below. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a 1.2-cm vegetation on the aortic valve. He is admitted and started on intravenous antibiotics. After 10 days, his fevers persist, and he complains of increasing left upper quadrant abdominal pain. What is the most likely cause of his persistent symptoms? Hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL Hematocrit 30 percent Red Blood Cell Count 3.4 million/μL Mean Corpuscular Volume 88 fL Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin 29 pg White Blood Cell Count 11.200 /mm³ Neutrophils 72 percent Lymphocytes 20 percent Monocytes 6 percent Eosinophils 2 percent Platelet Count 280.000 /μL Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate 85 mm/hr Blood Culture Positive for Streptococcus bovis
explanation: Explanation This patient with infective endocarditis presents with persistent high fever and tender splenomegaly despite antibiotic therapy, raising suspicion for splenic abscess, a rare but life-threatening complication of bacteremia from infective endocarditis. Diagnosis is confirmed by CT scan of the abdomen; treatment generally requires antibiotic therapy plus splenectomy as many patients fail percutaneous aspiration. (Choice A) Splenic infarction Splenic infarction can occur in infective endocarditis due to septic emboli and may cause left upper quadrant pain and splenomegaly. However, splenic infarction typically causes acute severe pain that gradually improves, whereas this patient has persistent high fever and progressively worsening pain despite antibiotic therapy, which is more characteristic of an infectious process like splenic abscess. (Choice B) Renal abscess Renal abscess can occur as a complication of bacteremia from infective endocarditis and would cause persistent fever. However, it typically presents with flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, and urinary symptoms rather than the left upper quadrant pain and tender splenomegaly described in this case. (Choice C) Cerebral abscess Cerebral abscess is a possible embolic complication of infective endocarditis but typically presents with neurological symptoms such as headache, altered mental status, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits. The patient's presentation of left upper quadrant pain with tender splenomegaly points to an intra-abdominal process rather than a neurologic complication. (Choice D) Splenic abscess Splenic abscess is a rare complication of bacteremia from infective endocarditis, manifesting as persistent high fever and tender splenomegaly despite antibiotic therapy. It requires CT diagnosis and often antibiotics plus splenectomy. (Choice E) Hepatic abscess Hepatic abscess could cause persistent fever and abdominal pain in the setting of bacteremia, but it typically presents with right upper quadrant pain and tenderness. The patient's left upper quadrant pain and prominent splenomegaly are inconsistent with a hepatic process.

question: A 68-year-old man with a history of chronic dyspepsia presents to the emergency department with complaints of progressive fatigue, nausea, confusion, and decreased urine output over the past week. He reports self-medicating with over-the-counter antacids, consuming up to 10 tablets daily for the last month to manage his symptoms while working long hours as a truck driver. His vital signs are normal except for mild hypertension. Laboratory values are shown below. What is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation? Serum Calcium 12.8 mg/dL Serum Creatinine 2.4 mg/dL Bicarbonate (HCO3-) 34 mEq/L Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) 8 pg/mL Arterial pH 7.48 Sodium 140 mEq/L Potassium 4.2 mEq/L Chloride 102 mEq/L Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) 18 mg/dL Glucose 95 mg/dL Total Protein 7.0 g/dL Albumin 3.8 g/dL AST 22 U/L ALT 25 U/L Alkaline Phosphatase 80 U/L
explanation: Explanation The patient has milk-alkali syndrome from excessive calcium carbonate antacid intake, presenting with the classic triad of hypercalcemia (12.8 mg/dL), metabolic alkalosis (HCO3- 34 mEq/L, pH 7.48), and acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.4 mg/dL). The suppressed PTH (8 pg/mL) confirms the calcium excess is exogenous. Hypercalcemia causes renal vasoconstriction and decreased GFR, while the carbonate component provides the alkali load. This syndrome has become more common with widespread use of calcium carbonate for heartburn and osteoporosis prevention. (Choice A) Thiazide diuretic use This is incorrect. Thiazide diuretics can cause mild hypercalcemia by increasing distal tubular calcium reabsorption, but the degree is typically modest (rarely >11.5 mg/dL). Thiazides do not cause the severe hypercalcemia, metabolic alkalosis, or acute kidney injury pattern seen in this patient, nor is there any history of thiazide use. (Choice B) Hypervitaminosis D This is incorrect. While vitamin D intoxication can cause hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH and kidney injury, it does not cause metabolic alkalosis. The patient's clear history of excessive calcium carbonate antacid use (10 tablets daily for one month) and the classic triad of findings point specifically to milk-alkali syndrome rather than vitamin D excess. (Choice C) Excessive calcium carbonate intake This is correct. The patient's excessive use of calcium carbonate antacids has led to milk-alkali syndrome, presenting with the triad of hypercalcemia, metabolic alkalosis, and acute kidney injury, along with suppressed PTH. (Choice D) Primary hyperparathyroidism This is incorrect. Primary hyperparathyroidism typically causes hypercalcemia with elevated or inappropriately normal PTH (>20 pg/mL), not suppressed PTH as seen here (8 pg/mL). Additionally, primary hyperparathyroidism rarely causes the combination of metabolic alkalosis and acute kidney injury seen in this patient. (Choice E) Malignancy-associated hypercalcemia This is incorrect. Malignancy-associated hypercalcemia typically involves elevated PTH-related peptide (PTHrP) with suppressed PTH and can cause kidney injury. However, metabolic alkalosis is not a feature of malignancy-associated hypercalcemia, and there is no clinical history or laboratory findings suggestive of malignancy in this patient.

question: A 65-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit with septic shock. The attending physician verbally orders 'administer 500 mg of levofloxacin IV now' to the nurse over the phone during a busy shift. The nurse mishears the order as 'administer 500 mg of levetiracetam IV now' and administers the anticonvulsant instead of the antibiotic. The patient's condition worsens due to delayed appropriate antimicrobial therapy. An investigation reveals that the error stemmed from phonetic similarity between the drug names and the verbal nature of the order without confirmation. Which of the following strategies, if implemented, would most likely have prevented this medication error?

answers.label: A
answers.text: Practicing closed-loop communication for verbal orders (82.47%)

answers.label: B
answers.text: Conducting annual staff training on look-alike/sound-alike medications (0%)

answers.label: C
answers.text: Implementing mandatory electronic prescribing for all orders (8.25%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Applying high-alert warning labels to similar-sounding medications (8.25%)

answers.label: E
answers.text: Utilizing standardized checklists for all medication administrations (1.03%)

explanation: Explanation Use of closed-loop communication would have identified and corrected this miscommunicated verbal order, preventing the incorrect administration of levetiracetam instead of levofloxacin. Other strategies such as electronic prescribing, warning labels, staff training, or checklists would not have directly prevented this specific verbal miscommunication error. (Choice A) Practicing closed-loop communication for verbal orders Closed-loop communication involves the receiver repeating back the order to the giver for confirmation, which would have clarified the misheard drug name and prevented the error. (Choice B) Conducting annual staff training on look-alike/sound-alike medications Annual training on look-alike/sound-alike medications increases staff awareness and recognition of high-risk drug pairs, but it does not provide a real-time mechanism to catch and correct verbal miscommunications as they occur during order transmission. (Choice C) Implementing mandatory electronic prescribing for all orders While electronic prescribing significantly reduces errors from illegible handwriting and automatically checks for drug interactions, it would not prevent errors in urgent verbal orders given over the phone during critical situations like septic shock management. (Choice D) Applying high-alert warning labels to similar-sounding medications High-alert warning labels on look-alike/sound-alike medication packages are helpful during the dispensing and administration phases, but they cannot address the fundamental miscommunication that occurred during the initial verbal order transmission. (Choice E) Utilizing standardized checklists for all medication administrations Standardized medication administration checklists improve the verification process during drug preparation and administration, but they would not catch an error that originated from mishearing the drug name during the initial verbal order, as the wrong drug would already be documented.

question: A 32-year-old man with a known history of hemophilia B presents to the clinic with progressive pain and stiffness in his left elbow. He reports a lifelong history of easy bruising and spontaneous joint bleeds, particularly in his elbows and knees, but admits to inconsistent adherence to prophylactic factor IX infusions due to financial constraints. Physical examination reveals limited range of motion in the affected elbow with crepitus and mild swelling. Radiographs are shown below. Which of the following best describes the primary pathophysiological mechanism underlying this patient's chronic joint damage?

answers.label: A
answers.text: Urate crystal deposition and tophus formation (0%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Amyloid protein accumulation and villonodular synovitis (0%)

explanation: Explanation This patient with hemophilia B has developed hemophilic arthropathy due to recurrent hemarthroses in his elbow. The condition arises from repeated intra-articular bleeding, leading to hemosiderin deposition within the synovium, which triggers chronic inflammation, synovial hypertrophy, fibrosis, and eventual destruction of cartilage and bone. Prophylactic factor replacement therapy can significantly reduce the risk of such complications by preventing bleeding episodes. (Choice A) Urate crystal deposition and tophus formation This describes gouty arthritis caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition in joints. While gout can cause chronic joint damage, it is unrelated to bleeding disorders and would present with acute attacks of severe joint pain, typically affecting the first metatarsophalangeal joint initially. (Choice B) Bacterial invasion and septic synovitis Septic arthritis involves bacterial infection of the joint space causing acute purulent synovitis. This patient's chronic, progressive course without fever or acute inflammatory signs, combined with his bleeding disorder history, makes infectious etiology unlikely. (Choice C) Calcium pyrophosphate deposition and chondrocalcinosis This refers to pseudogout or calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, which can cause joint inflammation but is not associated with hemophilia or recurrent bleeding. (Choice D) Amyloid protein accumulation and villonodular synovitis Pigmented villonodular synovitis (PVNS) is a benign proliferative disorder of synovial tissue that can cause joint destruction. While PVNS can involve hemosiderin deposition, it is not caused by recurrent bleeding episodes and typically presents as a monoarticular process in younger adults without underlying bleeding disorders. (Choice E) Hemosiderin deposition and fibrosis Recurrent hemarthroses in hemophilia lead to iron (hemosiderin) accumulation in the synovium, causing chronic synovitis, fibrosis, and progressive joint destruction.

question: A 38-week male neonate is born to a 29-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 9.4% at 34 weeks). Birth weight is 4,620 g (large for gestational age). Apgar scores are 8 and 9. At 1 hour of life, the infant appears jittery with poor feeding. Vital signs are normal. Point-of-care blood glucose is 28 mg/dL. The infant is unable to latch effectively for breastfeeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.label: B
answers.text: Reassure the mother and recheck blood glucose in 2 hours (0%)

answers.label: C
answers.text: Administer IV dextrose and begin continuous dextrose infusion (100%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Administer oral dextrose gel and retry breastfeeding (0%)

answers.label: E
answers.text: Order a serum insulin level and cortisol before initiating any treatment (0%)

explanation: Explanation Infants of diabetic mothers are at high risk for neonatal hypoglycemia due to fetal hyperinsulinism driven by chronic maternal hyperglycemia. When symptomatic hypoglycemia is present (glucose <40 mg/dL with clinical signs) and oral feeding is ineffective, IV dextrose is the treatment of choice. Early glucose monitoring and feeding support are essential in this population to prevent neurologic injury. (Choice A) Administer glucagon 0.3 mg intramuscularly While glucagon can transiently raise glucose by stimulating hepatic glycogenolysis, it has limited efficacy in neonates because glycogen stores are often inadequate, particularly in IDMs who may have depleted stores due to the metabolic demands of macrosomia. Additionally, the standard neonatal dose is 0.3 mg IM, not 0.5 mg. IV dextrose provides more predictable and sustained glucose elevation and is the preferred first-line treatment for symptomatic neonatal hypoglycemia. Glucagon is generally reserved as an adjunct when IV access cannot be established immediately. (Choice B) Reassure the mother and recheck blood glucose in 2 hours This infant has symptomatic hypoglycemia (jitteriness, glucose 28 mg/dL), which requires immediate intervention. The combination of symptoms and glucose <40 mg/dL meets criteria for urgent treatment. Waiting 2 hours without treatment risks prolonged hypoglycemia and potential neurologic injury, including seizures and long-term developmental sequelae. Watchful waiting is only appropriate for asymptomatic neonates with glucose levels 25-40 mg/dL who can feed effectively. (Choice C) Administer IV dextrose and begin continuous dextrose infusion This infant of a diabetic mother (IDM) has symptomatic hypoglycemia (glucose 28 mg/dL with jitteriness) and is unable to feed effectively, making IV dextrose the correct intervention. During gestation, chronic maternal hyperglycemia causes fetal hyperinsulinemia; at birth, maternal glucose supply ceases abruptly but fetal insulin levels remain elevated, precipitating hypoglycemia. For symptomatic neonates or those with glucose <40-45 mg/dL who cannot feed enterally, a D10W bolus of 200 mg/kg (2 mL/kg of D10W) followed by a continuous glucose infusion rate of approximately 6-8 mg/kg/min is recommended. This approach rapidly corrects hypoglycemia and provides sustained glucose delivery while the infant's insulin levels normalize over the first 24-48 hours. Close monitoring every 30-60 minutes is required to ensure glucose stabilization and guide infusion rate adjustments. (Choice D) Administer oral dextrose gel and retry breastfeeding Dextrose gel is an appropriate intervention for asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic hypoglycemia in infants who can feed and have glucose levels in the 30-45 mg/dL range. However, this infant is symptomatic with active jitteriness and is unable to latch, making oral gel insufficient and potentially unsafe due to aspiration risk. IV dextrose is preferred for symptomatic neonatal hypoglycemia. (Choice E) Order a serum insulin level and cortisol before initiating any treatment While diagnostic workup including insulin, C-peptide, cortisol, and growth hormone levels may be valuable for evaluating persistent or recurrent hypoglycemia, treatment should never be delayed in a symptomatic neonate. These laboratory studies can be drawn during the hypoglycemic episode before treatment if desired, but should not precede immediate glucose administration. In this case, the etiology (infant of diabetic mother with transient hyperinsulinism) is clinically apparent, making extensive workup less urgent than immediate stabilization.

question: A 54-year-old woman presents to the neurology clinic with a 4-month history of progressive bilateral leg weakness, difficulty walking, and numbness in her feet. She underwent Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery 3 years ago and has been taking high-dose zinc supplements (150 mg/day) prescribed by a naturopath for immune support. Neurological examination reveals spastic paraparesis, hyperreflexia in the lower extremities, and impaired vibration sense in the feet bilaterally. MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine shows T2 signal hyperintensity in the posterior and lateral columns. Laboratory studies reveal: hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, MCV 108 fL, serum ceruloplasmin 8 mg/dL (normal 20–60 mg/dL), serum copper 42 mcg/dL (normal 70–140 mcg/dL), and serum zinc 210 mcg/dL (normal 60–120 mcg/dL). Which of the following best explains the mechanism by which this patient developed her neurological and hematologic findings?

answers.label: A
answers.text: Excess zinc induces intestinal metallothionein, which preferentially binds copper and prevents its absorption, leading to copper deficiency myelopathy and anemia (50%)

answers.label: B
answers.text: Zinc toxicity directly damages peripheral nerves and bone marrow, causing sensory neuropathy and anemia (0%)

answers.label: C
answers.text: Folate deficiency due to malabsorption after bariatric surgery causing megaloblastic anemia and myelopathy (0%)

answers.label: D
answers.text: Vitamin B12 malabsorption due to loss of intrinsic factor-producing parietal cells after gastric bypass (50%)

answers.label: E
answers.text: Iron deficiency anemia from reduced gastric acid impairing non-heme iron absorption after bypass (0%)

explanation: Explanation Excess zinc competitively inhibits intestinal copper absorption by inducing metallothionein, a protein that preferentially binds copper and sequesters it in enterocytes, leading to copper deficiency. Copper deficiency causes a myelopathy resembling subacute combined degeneration, with posterior and lateral column involvement, as well as sideroblastic anemia from impaired iron utilization. This presentation is seen classically in patients on high-dose zinc supplementation or following gastric bypass surgery. (Choice A) Excess zinc induces intestinal metallothionein, which preferentially binds copper and prevents its absorption, leading to copper deficiency myelopathy and anemia Zinc at high doses upregulates metallothionein synthesis in intestinal enterocytes.
